---3d:T178a,The RBI Act, 1934 comprises **Chapters I to V** alongside four primary **Schedules**:

### 1. Master Section Index: RBI Act, 1934

| Chapter & Section | Statutory Subject Matter | Key Legal Provision & Examination Point |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Chapter I: Sec 1 & 2** | Preliminary & Definitions | • **Sec 2(e):** Defines a **"Scheduled Bank"** as a bank included in the **Second Schedule** of the RBI Act. |
| **Chapter II: Sec 3** | Establishment of the Bank | Mandates establishment of the RBI to regulate bank notes, maintain reserves for monetary stability, and operate the currency and credit system. |
| **Chapter II: Sec 4** | Capital of the Bank | Original share capital was **₹5 Crore** divided into 5 lakh shares of ₹100 each. Entire capital nationalized by GoI on **1 January 1949**. |
| **Chapter II: Sec 7** | Central Government Directions | Empowers Central Government, after consultation with the Governor, to give directions to the RBI in the public interest. |
| **Chapter II: Sec 8** | Composition of Central Board | **21 Members:** Governor + up to 4 Deputy Governors (appointed by GoI for up to 5 yrs); 4 Directors from Local Boards; 10 Directors nominated by GoI; 2 Government officials. |
| **Chapter II: Sec 9** | Local Boards | Four Local Boards (Western, Eastern, Northern, Southern areas based in **Mumbai, Kolkata, New Delhi, Chennai**). 5 members each; 4-year term. |
| **Chapter II: Sec 17** | **Permitted Business of RBI** | • **17(1):** Accepting deposits without interest.<br>• **17(2):** Purchase, sale, and rediscount of commercial bills and export bills.<br>• **17(3):** Buying and selling foreign exchange.<br>• **17(4):** Short-term loans and advances to banks against approved collateral.<br>• **17(5):** **Ways and Means Advances (WMA)** to Central and State Govts (repayable within 3 months).<br>• **17(8):** Purchase and sale of Government Securities (OMO). |
| **Chapter II: Sec 18** | Emergency / Special Advances | Direct discounting of bills or loans to banks when normal financial channels are impaired (Lender of Last Resort). |
| **Chapter II: Sec 19** | **Prohibited Business of RBI** | RBI **CANNOT**: engage in direct trade; purchase its own shares or shares of other banks; make loans on mortgage of immovable property; grant unsecured advances; or **pay interest on deposits**. |
| **Chapter III: Sec 20 & 21** | Banker to Central Government | Obligation and right of the RBI to transact banking business of the Central Government. |
| **Chapter III: Sec 21A** | Banker to State Governments | RBI transacts banking business of State Governments by voluntary bilateral agreement. |
| **Chapter III: Sec 22** | **Sole Right to Issue Notes** | RBI possesses the exclusive monopoly to issue bank notes in India (except **₹1 notes and coins**, which are issued by the Ministry of Finance). |
| **Chapter III: Sec 24** | Denominations of Notes | Permitted denominations: ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500, ₹2000, or any other denomination **not exceeding ₹10,000** (*Note: ₹2000 remains a statutory denomination under Sec 24, though withdrawn from active circulation under Clean Note Policy on 19 May 2023*). |
| **Chapter III: Sec 26** | **Legal Tender Character** | • **26(1):** Every bank note is legal tender across India.<br>• **26(2):** Central Government, upon recommendation of the Central Board, can declare **any series of bank notes of any denomination to cease to be legal tender** (Statutory basis of Demonetisation). |
| **Chapter III: Sec 27** | Re-issue of Notes | Prohibits RBI from putting into re-circulation notes that are torn, defaced, or excessively soiled. |
| **Chapter III: Sec 28** | Recovery of Lost/Mutilated Notes | RBI is not bound to refund lost or stolen notes; governed by **RBI (Note Refund) Rules**. |
| **Chapter III: Sec 31** | Bearer Demand Bills | Restricts issue of demand bills/promissory notes payable to bearer exclusively to the RBI and Central Government. |
| **Chapter III: Sec 33** | **Minimum Reserve System** | Assets of Issue Department must not be less than **₹200 Crore** at any time: **Gold Bullion/Coins ≥ ₹115 Crore**; Foreign Securities make up the remaining balance (**₹85 Crore**). |
| **Chapter III: Sec 42** | **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** | • **42(1):** Mandates every Scheduled Bank to maintain with RBI an average daily balance of not less than a prescribed percentage of its Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL).<br>• Amendment 2006 **removed the statutory floor of 3% and ceiling of 20%**.<br>• **42(1A):** Incremental CRR (I-CRR) to impound excess liquidity surges.<br>• **42(6):** Qualifying conditions for inclusion in **Second Schedule**: Paid-up capital and reserves **≥ ₹5 Lakh**, and affairs not conducted to the detriment of depositors. |
| **Chapter IIIB: Sec 45-IA** | Regulation of NBFCs | Mandatory Certificate of Registration (CoR) and minimum Net Owned Funds (NOF) to commence NBFC business. |
| **Chapter IIIF: Sec 45ZA–ZN** | **Monetary Policy Framework** | • **45ZA:** Inflation target set once every 5 years ($4\% \pm 2\%$).<br>• **45ZB:** 6-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).<br>• **45ZG:** Quorum of 4 members.<br>• **45ZH:** At least 4 meetings per year.<br>• **45ZN:** Failure report if inflation breaches target for **3 consecutive quarters**. |
| **Chapter IV: Sec 47** | Allocation of Surplus Profits | After provisions for bad debts and depreciation, RBI transfers surplus net profits to the Central Government. |
| **Chapter IV: Sec 49** | Publication of Bank Rate | Mandates publication of standard rate at which RBI buys or rediscounts eligible bills. |
| **Schedules I to IV** | First to Fourth Schedules | • **First Schedule:** Four regional territories of Local Boards.<br>• **Second Schedule:** Master list of **Scheduled Commercial and Cooperative Banks**.<br>• **Third Schedule:** Declaration of secrecy by Board members.<br>• **Fourth Schedule:** Repealed provisions. |

---3e:T2cd5,The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 comprises **Sections 1 to 56** organized across **Parts I to V**:

### 1. Master Section Index: Banking Regulation Act, 1949

| Section Number | Statutory Subject Matter | Key Legal Mandate & Exam Significance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Sec 3** | Non-Applicability | The Act does NOT apply to Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) or Cooperative Land Mortgage Banks. |
| **Sec 5(b)** | **Definition of "Banking"** | *"Accepting, for the purpose of lending or investment, of deposits of money from the public, repayable on demand or otherwise, and withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise."* |
| **Sec 5(c)** | Definition of Banking Company | Any company which transacts the business of banking in India. |
| **Sec 6** | Permitted Forms of Business | Explicitly lists 17 permitted ancillary activities: borrowing, lending, discounting bills, issuing letters of credit, guarantees, underwriting, safety lockers, acting as agent/trustee, factoring. |
| **Sec 7** | Use of Words "Bank" / "Banker" | Every banking company must use at least one of the words **"bank"**, **"banker"**, **"banking"**, or **"banking company"** as part of its name. Non-banking entities are strictly prohibited from using these words. |
| **Sec 8** | **Prohibition of Trading** | No banking company shall directly or indirectly deal in buying, selling, or bartering of goods (except when realizing security pledged against debts). |
| **Sec 9** | **Disposal of Non-Banking Assets** | Any immovable property acquired by a bank in satisfaction of claims/debts must be disposed of within **7 years**. RBI may extend this period by up to **5 additional years**. |
| **Sec 10A to 10D** | Board of Directors Qualifications | At least **51% of Directors** must possess specialized knowledge or practical experience in accountancy, agriculture, banking, cooperation, economics, finance, law, or small-scale industries. |
| **Sec 12** | Capital Structure & Voting Rights | • Subscribed capital must be at least **50% of Authorized capital**.<br>• Paid-up capital must be at least **50% of Subscribed capital**.<br>• Voting rights of any single shareholder in private banks capped at **26%** by RBI. |
| **Sec 17** | **Statutory Reserve Fund** | Every banking company must transfer **not less than 20% of its net profit** (raised to **25% by RBI Master Direction**) of each year to a Reserve Fund before declaring any dividend. |
| **Sec 18** | Cash Reserve for Non-Scheduled Banks | Non-scheduled banks must maintain a cash reserve of at least **3% of their NDTL** in cash or current account with the RBI. |
| **Sec 19** | **Restriction on Subsidiaries** | • Bank cannot form a subsidiary except for permitted activities under Sec 6.<br>• Bank cannot hold shares in any company exceeding **30% of that company's paid-up share capital + reserves**, OR **30% of the bank's own paid-up share capital + reserves**, whichever is less. |
| **Sec 20** | **Restrictions on Loans and Advances** | • Bank **CANNOT grant loans on the security of its own shares**.<br>• Bank cannot grant loans to its own Directors or firms/entities in which its Directors are interested (without prior Board/RBI approval). |
| **Sec 21** | Control over Advances by RBI | Empowers RBI to issue directions on credit policy, margins on secured loans, maximum exposure limits, and lending interest rates. |
| **Sec 21A** | Protection Against Scrutiny of Rates | Rates of interest charged by banks **cannot be reopened or scrutinized by courts** under the Usurious Loans Act, 1918. |
| **Sec 22** | **Licensing of Banking Companies** | Mandatory requirement to obtain a **License from the RBI** before commencing or carrying on banking business in India. |
| **Sec 23** | Branch Licensing | Prior permission of RBI required for opening a new place of business or changing existing locations. |
| **Sec 24** | **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** | Every banking company must maintain liquid assets (cash, gold, or unencumbered approved G-Secs) equal to a prescribed percentage of its NDTL (Statutory ceiling: **40%**; floor of 25% eliminated in 2007). |
| **Sec 26** | Return of Unclaimed Deposits | Mandates annual return of all deposit accounts that have not been operated for **10 years**. |
| **Sec 26A** | **Depositor Education & Awareness (DEA) Fund** | All bank deposits and balances remaining unclaimed for **over 10 years** must be credited to the DEA Fund within 3 months. Depositors can claim their refunds with interest at any subsequent time. |
| **Sec 29 & 30** | Accounts, Balance Sheet & Audit | • **Sec 29:** Preparation of Balance Sheet (Form A) and Profit & Loss Account (Form B) as on **31 March** under the **Third Schedule**.<br>• **Sec 30:** Mandatory audit by a qualified Chartered Accountant; appointment/re-appointment requires prior approval of the RBI. |
| **Sec 31** | Submission of Audited Returns | Three copies of audited balance sheet and P&L account submitted to RBI within **3 months** from the end of the accounting period. |
| **Sec 35** | **Inspection by RBI** | Empowers RBI to conduct on-site inspection of books and accounts of any banking company; report submitted to Central Government. |
| **Sec 35A** | **Power to Issue Directions** | Apex power of RBI to issue directions to banks in the **public interest**, in the interest of banking policy, or to prevent the affairs of any bank being conducted detrimentally to depositors. |
| **Sec 35AA & 35AB** | Insolvency Resolution Directions | Empowers Central Govt to authorize RBI to direct banks to initiate corporate insolvency resolution under the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016**. |
| **Sec 36AA** | **Removal of Managerial Personnel** | RBI may remove any Chairman, Director, CEO, or employee of a bank if satisfied their continuation is detrimental to depositors. |
| **Sec 36AB** | Appointment of Additional Directors | RBI may appoint up to **5 additional directors** on the Board of a banking company. |
| **Sec 36ACA** | **Supersession of Board of Directors** | RBI may supersede the Board of Directors of a banking company for a period up to **12 months** and appoint an Administrator. |
| **Sec 45** | **Moratorium & Compulsory Amalgamation** | • RBI can apply to Central Govt for order of **Moratorium (up to 6 months)** on a failing bank.<br>• During moratorium, RBI prepares a scheme of reconstruction or **compulsory amalgamation** with another bank (e.g., Yes Bank reconstruction; amalgamation of Lakshmi Vilas Bank into DBS Bank India). |
| **Sec 56** | **Application to Co-operative Banks** | Applies provisions of BR Act to Primary Co-operative Banks (UCBs), State Co-operative Banks, and DCCBs. Substantially expanded by the **Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020** to give RBI direct regulatory control over UCB management, audit, and resolution. |

### Examiner Trap Vault: Unit 22 High-Yield Distractors

1. **Trap — Note Issuance Authority:** The ₹1 note and metallic coins are issued by the **Ministry of Finance (Government of India)**, bearing the signature of the **Finance Secretary**. Bank notes of ₹2 and above are issued by the **RBI under Section 22**, bearing the signature of the **RBI Governor**.
2. **Trap — Prohibited Banking Business:** Under Section 19 of the RBI Act, the RBI **CANNOT pay interest on deposits** placed with it, and under Section 8 of the BR Act, a commercial bank **CANNOT engage in buying and selling goods (trading)**.
3. **Trap — Non-Banking Asset Disposal Period:** Under Section 9 of the BR Act, immovable property acquired by a bank must be disposed of within **7 years** (RBI can grant an extension of up to **5 years**). Total maximum holding period is **12 years**.
4. **Trap — Statutory Reserve Fund Transfer:** Section 17 of the BR Act specifies **20% of net profits**, but the RBI's Master Direction mandates a higher prudential transfer of **25% of net profits**.
5. **Trap — Loan on Own Shares:** Under Section 20 of the BR Act, a bank is **STRICTLY PROHIBITED from granting any loan or advance against the security of its own shares**.
6. **Trap — Unclaimed Deposits Timeline:** Deposits inactive for **10 years** are transferred to the **DEA Fund under Section 26A** of the BR Act.

> **Core Proposition:** The Indian commercial banking structure comprises Public Sector Banks (PSBs), Private Sector Banks, and Foreign Banks. Indian banks must maintain a minimum Total Capital (CRAR) of 11.5% (including a 2.5% Capital Conservation Buffer). Breach of capital, asset quality (Net NPA ≥ 6%), or leverage triggers Prompt Corrective Action (PCA).

### 1. Structure of Scheduled Commercial Banks in India

| Banking Category | Institutional Composition & Numbers | Operating Charter & Regulatory Status |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Public Sector Banks (PSBs)** | **12 Banks:** State Bank of India (SBI) + 11 Nationalized Banks (PNB, BoB, Canara, Union, etc.) | Governed by SBI Act, 1955 and Banking Companies (Acquisition & Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970/1980. Central Government holds majority (> 51%) equity. |
| **Private Sector Banks** | • *Old Private Banks:* Established prior to 1993 (Federal Bank, South Indian Bank, CSB).<br>• *New Private Banks:* Established post-1993 reforms (HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank). | Incorporated under Companies Act, licensed under Section 22 of Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Majority equity held by private investors and institutional funds. |
| **Foreign Banks in India** | Banks incorporated overseas operating in India via **Branch Mode** or **Wholly Owned Subsidiary (WOS) Mode** (Standard Chartered, Citibank, HSBC, DBS Bank India). | Subject to full domestic regulation, CRAR, and Priority Sector Lending (PSL) mandates. |

### 2. Basel III Capital Adequacy Architecture (RBI Master Directions)

The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) formulated Basel III following the 2008 crisis. The Reserve Bank of India enforced **more stringent capital standards than the global Basel III baseline**:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 INDIAN BASEL III REGULATORY CAPITAL ARCHITECTURE            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────┬───────────────┤
│ CAPITAL COMPONENT                               │ BCBS BASE │ RBI MANDATE   │
│ • Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1)                   │ 4.5%      │ 5.5% of RWAs  │
│ • Total Tier 1 Capital                          │ 6.0%      │ 7.0% of RWAs  │
│ • Minimum Total Capital (CRAR without CCB)      │ 8.0%      │ 9.0% of RWAs  │
│ • Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB - pure CET1) │ 2.5%      │ 2.5% of RWAs  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────┼───────────────┤
│ TOTAL MINIMUM CAPITAL (INCLUDING CCB)           │ 10.5%     │ 11.5% of RWAs │
│ • Maximum Allowable Tier 2 Capital              │ 2.0%      │ 2.0% of RWAs  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────┴───────────────┘
```

• **Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) Formula:**
  $$\text{CRAR} = \frac{\text{Eligible Tier 1 Capital} + \text{Eligible Tier 2 Capital}}{\text{Credit Risk RWAs} + \text{Market Risk RWAs} + \text{Operational Risk RWAs}} \ge 11.5\%$$

• **Tier 1 Capital (Going-Concern Capital):** Absorbs losses while the bank remains solvent and operational. Comprises **CET1** (paid-up equity shares, statutory reserves, retained earnings) and **Additional Tier 1 (AT1)** capital (Perpetual Non-Cumulative Preference Shares, PNCPS; Perpetual Debt Instruments with statutory loss-absorption write-down/conversion clauses).  
• **Tier 2 Capital (Gone-Concern Capital):** Absorbs losses in the event of winding up or liquidation. Comprises general provisions for standard assets (up to 1.25% of credit RWAs), revaluation reserves (at a 55% discount), and subordinated debt instruments (minimum maturity 5 years). Capped at **2.0% of RWAs**.  
• **Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs):**
  - Banks classified as "Too Big to Fail" based on Size, Interconnectedness, Lack of Substitutability, and Complexity.
  - Currently identified D-SIBs: **State Bank of India (SBI)**, **HDFC Bank**, and **ICICI Bank**.
  - Subject to an additional **CET1 capital surcharge** ranging from 0.20% to 0.80% of RWAs.
• **Basel III Liquidity Standards:**
  - **Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR):** Mandates holding sufficient unencumbered High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) to survive a 30-day severe liquidity stress scenario:
    $$\text{LCR} = \frac{\text{Total Stock of HQLA}}{\text{Total Net Cash Outflows over 30 Days}} \ge 100\%$$
  - **Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR):** Promotes medium/long-term funding stability over a 1-year horizon:
    $$\text{NSFR} = \frac{\text{Available Stable Funding (ASF)}}{\text{Required Stable Funding (RSF)}} \ge 100\%$$
  - **Leverage Ratio:** Non-risk-based backstop: $\frac{\text{Tier 1 Capital}}{\text{Total Exposure}} \ge 3.5\%$ (4.0% for D-SIBs).

---

### 3. Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework (RBI Framework Effective 1 Jan 2022)

The RBI's **Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework for Scheduled Commercial Banks** (Circular dated 2 Nov 2021, effective 1 Jan 2022) monitors banks across three parameters: **Capital, Asset Quality, and Leverage**.

> **Methodology — Basis-Point Deterioration from Capital Baseline:**  
> In the RBI 2022 framework, PCA capital thresholds are officially measured by **basis-point (bps) deterioration from the applicable regulatory minimum including the Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB)**:
> • Baseline CRAR = **11.5%** (9.0% regulatory minimum + 2.5% CCB).  
> • Baseline CET1 = **8.0%** (5.5% regulatory minimum + 2.5% CCB).

| Parameter & Indicator | Applicable Regulatory Baseline (incl. CCB) | Risk Threshold 1 (Mandatory Dividend Curbs) | Risk Threshold 2 (Threshold 1 + Branch Curbs) | Risk Threshold 3 (Threshold 2 + Remuneration Curbs) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **CRAR (Total Capital)** | **11.5%**<br>*(9.0% min + 2.5% CCB)* | **Up to 250 bps below baseline**<br>*(≥ 9.0% to < 11.5%)* | **> 250 bps to ≤ 400 bps below baseline**<br>*(≥ 7.5% to < 9.0%)* | **> 400 bps below baseline**<br>*(< 7.5%)* |
| **Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1)** | **8.0%**<br>*(5.5% min + 2.5% CCB)* | **Up to 162.5 bps below baseline**<br>*(≥ 6.375% to < 8.0%)* | **> 162.5 bps to ≤ 312.5 bps below baseline**<br>*(≥ 4.875% to < 6.375%)* | **> 312.5 bps below baseline**<br>*(< 4.875%)* |
| **Asset Quality (Net NPA Ratio)** | **< 6.0%** | **≥ 6.0% to < 9.0%** | **≥ 9.0% to < 12.0%** | **≥ 12.0%** |
| **Tier 1 Leverage Ratio** | **3.5%** (Other SCBs)<br>**4.0%** (D-SIBs) | **Up to 50 bps below min**<br>*(3.0% to < 3.5% Other; 3.5% to < 4.0% D-SIBs)* | **> 50 bps to ≤ 100 bps below min**<br>*(2.5% to < 3.0% Other; 3.0% to < 3.5% D-SIBs)* | **> 100 bps below min**<br>*(< 2.5% Other; < 3.0% D-SIBs)* |

> **Critical Supervisory Evolution:**  
> • **Removal of RoA Trigger:** In the revised PCA framework, **Return on Assets (RoA) was officially removed** as a mandatory supervisory trigger.  
> • **Mandatory Corrective Sanctions:**
>   - *Risk Threshold 1:* Mandatory restriction on dividend distribution and remittance of profits; promoters/owners mandated to infuse fresh capital.
>   - *Risk Threshold 2:* Threshold 1 restrictions PLUS mandatory prohibition on opening new domestic or overseas branches.
>   - *Risk Threshold 3:* Threshold 1 & 2 restrictions PLUS mandatory restriction on management compensation and directors' fees.
> • **Discretionary Actions:** Special supervisory inspection, credit portfolio caps, cessation of high-risk lending, or invoking merger/amalgamation under Section 45 of BR Act.

---

### Examiner Trap Vault: Unit 21 High-Yield Distractors

1. **Trap — Indian vs BCBS Minimum CRAR:** The Basel Committee (BCBS) baseline minimum CRAR is **8.0%** (10.5% with CCB). The Reserve Bank of India mandates a stricter minimum of **9.0%** (which reaches **11.5% with the 2.5% CCB**). An answer citing 9% as total capital including CCB is **incorrect**.
2. **Trap — Asset Quality PCA Trigger:** The PCA asset quality trigger is based strictly on the **Net NPA Ratio (≥ 6.0%)**, NOT the Gross NPA ratio.
3. **Trap — RoA in Revised PCA:** Return on Assets (RoA) is **NO LONGER a trigger** under the revised PCA framework for commercial banks.
4. **Trap — Tier 2 Capital Cap:** Under Basel III, eligible Tier 2 capital is capped at a maximum of **2.0% of Risk-Weighted Assets (RWAs)**.
5. **Trap — Current D-SIBs:** The three designated Domestic Systemically Important Banks in India are **SBI, HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank**.
6. **Trap — PCA Capital Trigger Calibration:** PCA thresholds are measured as basis-point deterioration from the **regulatory baseline including CCB (11.5% CRAR / 8.0% CET1)**. Total CRAR Threshold 1 triggers at up to 250 bps below 11.5% (i.e. **9.0% to < 11.5%**); Threshold 2 is **7.5% to < 9.0%**; Threshold 3 is **< 7.5%**. For CET1, Threshold 1 is **6.375% to < 8.0%**; Threshold 2 is **4.875% to < 6.375%**; Threshold 3 is **< 4.875%**.

### Answer Key & Explanations

• **Q1 — Answer: C.** The RBI mandates a minimum Total CRAR of 9.0% plus a Capital Conservation Buffer of 2.5%, totaling **11.5% of RWAs** (higher than the global BCBS baseline of 10.5%).  
• **Q2 — Answer: B.** Under the revised PCA framework, Risk Threshold 1 is triggered when the Net NPA ratio is $\ge 6.0\%$ but $< 9.0\%$.  
• **Q3 — Answer: A.** Statement I is correct (LCR $\ge 100\%$ for 30-day stress). Statement II is incorrect because the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) is a medium/long-term structural metric covering a **1-year horizon**, not an intraday metric.  
• **Q4 — Answer: C.** In the revised PCA framework, Return on Assets (RoA) was removed as an independent trigger to avoid penalizing temporarily unprofitable banks that maintain sound capital and low net NPAs.40:T2778,> **Curriculum Alignment — Official IIBF Paper 1 Benchmark (Unit 21b)**  
> **Core Proposition:** Differentiated banks operate under targeted mandates. RRBs focus on rural credit (75% PSL target, 50:15:35 shareholding). Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) are organized into a 4-Tier scale-based structure under the amended Banking Regulation Act, with a revised 60% PSL target. Small Finance Banks extend small credit (75% PSL), while Payment Banks handle payments and deposits (capped at ₹2 Lakh) with a strict prohibition on lending.

### 1. Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) Statutory Architecture

• **Legislative Enactment:** Established under the **Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976** (following the Narasimham Working Group recommendations; first RRB, *Prathama Bank* in Moradabad, UP, was established on 2 October 1975, sponsored by Syndicate Bank).  
• **Statutory Shareholding Distribution (Section 6, RRB Act):**
  $$\text{Central Government: } \mathbf{50\%} \quad\Big|\quad \text{Sponsor Commercial Bank: } \mathbf{35\%} \quad\Big|\quad \text{State Government: } \mathbf{15\%}$$
• **Supervision & Regulation:** Regulated by the **Reserve Bank of India** under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and statutorily inspected and supervised by **NABARD** under Section 35 of the BR Act.  
• **Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Mandate:** RRBs are mandated to achieve a total PSL target of **75% of ANBC or CEOBE**, with 18% dedicated to Agriculture (10% to Small & Marginal Farmers) and 15% to Weaker Sections.  
• **Capital Adequacy:** Mandated to maintain a minimum **CRAR of 9.0%**.

---

### 2. Primary Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs): The 4-Tier Regulatory Framework

Following the recommendations of the **N.S. Vishwanathan Expert Committee (2022)**, the RBI instituted a four-tiered regulatory framework based on deposit size to apply proportional regulation across UCBs:

| Tier Classification | Deposit Size Threshold | Minimum Net Worth Requirement | Mandatory CRAR Requirement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Tier 1 UCBs** | Deposits **up to ₹100 Crore** | • **₹2 Crore** (for unit UCBs operating in a single district)<br>• **₹5 Crore** (for all other UCBs) | **9.0%** (Standard baseline capital) |
| **Tier 2 UCBs** | Deposits **> ₹100 Crore and up to ₹1,000 Crore** | **₹5 Crore** | **12.0%** (Phased compliance) |
| **Tier 3 UCBs** | Deposits **> ₹1,000 Crore and up to ₹10,000 Crore** | **₹5 Crore** | **12.0%** |
| **Tier 4 UCBs** | Deposits **exceeding ₹10,000 Crore** | **₹5 Crore** | **12.0%** (Subject to comprehensive bank-like controls) |

> **Critical Regulatory Update — UCB Priority Sector Lending (PSL):**  
> Under the RBI's revised directions, the overall Priority Sector Lending target for Primary Urban Co-operative Banks is set at **60% of ANBC or CEOBE** (moderated from the earlier 75% aspirational path to preserve lending stability across municipal and cooperative centers).

• **Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 & UCB Governance:**
  - Resolved the historic "Dual Control" friction between State Registrars of Co-operative Societies (RCS) and the RBI.
  - Empowered RBI with direct statutory authority over UCBs regarding:
    1. Licensing, management appointments, and CEO qualifications under fit-and-proper criteria.
    2. Powers to supersede the Board of Directors of a cooperative bank for up to 5 years (under Section 56).
    3. Directing statutory audits by professional chartered accountants.
    4. Formulating schemes of reconstruction or amalgamation under Section 45 without placing the bank under initial moratorium.

---

### 3. Niche Differentiated Banks: Small Finance Banks vs. Payment Banks

Following the recommendations of the **Committee on Comprehensive Financial Services for Small Businesses and Low Income Households (Chaired by Dr. Nachiket Mor, 2014)**, the RBI introduced two differentiated banking licenses:

| Parameter | Small Finance Banks (SFBs) | Payment Banks (PBs) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Objective** | Financial inclusion through **savings mobilization and small credit delivery** to unserved segments. | Financial inclusion through **high-volume, low-value payments, remittances, and savings**. |
| **Minimum Paid-Up Capital** | **₹200 Crore** (₹100 Crore for UCBs voluntarily converting into SFBs) | **₹100 Crore** |
| **Lending Activity** | **PERMITTED** across retail, agriculture, MSME, and microfinance segments. | **STRICTLY PROHIBITED:** **Cannot lend, cannot grant loans, cannot issue credit cards!** |
| **Permitted Deposits** | Both Demand Deposits (CASA) and Time Deposits (FD/RD) without statutory ceiling. | **Demand Deposits only** (Savings & Current). Maximum balance: **₹2,00,000 per customer**. |
| **Portfolio Loan Restrictions** | At least **50% of total loan portfolio must comprise loans up to ₹25 Lakh**. | N/A (Zero loans permitted). |
| **Rural Branch Mandate** | At least **25% of physical branches must be in unbanked rural centres** (population < 10,000). | At least **25% of physical access points must be in unbanked rural centres**. |
| **Priority Sector Lending (PSL)** | **75% of ANBC or CEOBE** | N/A |
| **Capital Adequacy (CRAR)** | Minimum **15.0% of RWAs** (Tier 1 min 7.5%) | Minimum **15.0% of RWAs** |
| **Statutory Liquidity Deployment** | Normal CRR and SLR requirements. | • Mandatory CRR with RBI.<br>• Must invest **minimum 75% of demand deposits in G-Secs/T-Bills** (up to 1 yr tenor).<br>• Remaining max 25% in current/term deposits with SCBs. |
| **Promoter Lock-in** | Minimum 40% promoter equity locked for 5 years. | Minimum 40% promoter equity locked for 5 years. |

---

### 4. Local Area Banks (LABs) Architecture

• **Origin & Policy Mandate:** Introduced in **August 1996** following the 1996 Union Budget to mobilize rural and semi-urban household savings and channel local resources into local investments.  
• **Statutory & Operational Boundaries:**  
  - **Geographical Jurisdiction:** Strictly restricted to operate across a maximum of **three contiguous districts**.  
  - **Capital Requirement:** Minimum paid-up equity capital of **₹5 Crore** (with promoters contributing at least ₹2 Crore).  
  - **Regulatory Status:** Licensed under Section 22 of Banking Regulation Act, 1949 as Non-Scheduled Commercial Banks; mandated to maintain **15.0% CRAR** and comply with prudential priority sector norms. Active surviving LABs include *Coastal Local Area Bank Ltd* and *Krishna Bhima Samruddhi LAB Ltd*.

### Examiner Trap Vault: Unit 21b High-Yield Distractors

1. **Trap — Payment Bank Credit Cards:** Payment Banks **CANNOT issue Credit Cards**. They can issue ATM/Debit cards, Net Banking, and UPI handles, but **zero credit products**.
2. **Trap — Payment Bank Deposit Ceiling:** The maximum balance limit per customer in a Payment Bank is **₹2,00,000** (raised by RBI from the initial ₹1,00,000 limit in April 2021).
3. **Trap — RRB Shareholding Breakdown:** Central Government: **50%**, Sponsor Bank: **35%**, State Government: **15%**. (Do not confuse the Sponsor Bank's 35% with the State's 15%).
4. **Trap — UCB 2025 PSL Target:** In current RBI Master Directions, the overall PSL target for Urban Co-operative Banks is **60% of ANBC**, NOT 75% or 40%.
5. **Trap — Small Finance Bank Small Loan Quota:** An SFB must ensure that at least **50% of its loan portfolio comprises loans up to ₹25 Lakh**.
6. **Trap — Local Area Bank Jurisdiction:** LABs are restricted to a maximum of **3 contiguous districts** with minimum capital of **₹5 Crore**; they are NOT multi-state scheduled banks.

> **Core Proposition:** Microfinance delivers collateral-free credit to low-income households. The unified 2022 RBI regulatory framework applies activity-based standards across all lenders, establishing an annual household income cap of ₹3,00,000, a 50% debt-service outflow ceiling, and zero prepayment penalties.

### 1. Delivery Models in Indian Microfinance

• **Self-Help Group – Bank Linkage Programme (SBLP):**
  - Pioneered by **NABARD in 1992** based on the recommendations of the **S.K. Kalia Committee**.
  - A homogeneous group of **10 to 20 rural individuals** (primarily women) pooling periodic small savings into a common fund.
  - After 6 months of successful internal lending, commercial banks extend collateral-free credit linked to savings (scaling from 1:1 up to 1:4 or higher).
• **Joint Liability Groups (JLGs):**
  - An informal group of **4 to 10 individuals** borrowing funds from banks or MFIs under mutual co-guarantee without requiring prior joint savings.

### 2. RBI Harmonized Regulatory Framework for Microfinance Loans (Effective 1 April 2022)

This framework replaced all previous entity-specific guidelines with an activity-based regulation across ALL Regulated Entities (Commercial Banks, SFBs, RRBs, Co-op Banks, NBFCs, NBFC-MFIs):

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 CORE MANDATES OF THE 2022 RBI MICROFINANCE RULES            │
│                                                                             │
│  1. HOUSEHOLD INCOME CEILING  :  ₹3,00,000 per annum (Urban & Rural)        │
│  2. COLLATERAL REQUIREMENT    :  STRICTLY COLLATERAL-FREE (Zero security)    │
│  3. DEBT-SERVICE OUTFLOW CAP  :  MAXIMUM 50% of monthly household income    │
│  4. PREPAYMENT PENALTY        :  STRICTLY ZERO (Foreclosure fees banned)     │
│  5. NBFC-MFI QUALIFYING ASSETS:  Minimum 75% of total assets (down from 85%)│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

• **Assessment of Household Income:** A "Household" is defined as an individual unit comprising husband, wife, and their unmarried children. Lenders must conduct a verified board-approved income assessment.  
• **Limit on Outflow (Debt Servicing Burden):** Regulated entities cannot sanction a microfinance loan if the total monthly debt repayment (principal + interest across all existing loans) exceeds **50% of total monthly household income**.  
• **Pricing of Credit:** RBI dismantled the previously prescribed interest rate caps and margin caps for NBFC-MFIs. Interest rates must be determined by a board-approved policy with a transparent component breakdown disclosed in the **Key Fact Statement (KFS)**.

> **Core Proposition:** NBFCs are registered under the Companies Act and regulated under Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act. They must pass the 50-50 Principal Business Test. Under the Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework, the Top 10 eligible NBFCs by asset size are automatically placed in the Upper Layer subject to bank-like regulations.

### 1. NBFCs vs. Commercial Banks Core Differences

| Parameter | Commercial Banks | Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Incorporation / Licensing** | Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (Section 22) | Companies Act, 2013 + RBI Act, 1934 (Section 45-IA) |
| **Demand Deposits (CASA)** | **Permitted** (Can accept savings & current deposits) | **Strictly PROHIBITED** (Cannot accept demand deposits) |
| **Payment & Settlement System** | Part of clearing system (Cheque issuance on self) | **Cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves**; not part of payment clearing system |
| **Deposit Insurance (DICGC)** | **Covered up to ₹5 Lakh per depositor** | **Zero deposit insurance cover** (Deposits with NBFCs are NOT insured by DICGC) |
| **Statutory Reserves** | Mandatory CRR & SLR | No CRR; Deposit-taking NBFCs maintain liquid assets (15% of public deposits in approved securities) |

• **The 50-50 Principal Business Test:** An entity qualifies as an NBFC if its **financial assets constitute more than 50% of its total assets**, AND its **income from financial assets constitutes more than 50% of its gross income**.

---

### 2. RBI Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) 4-Layer Pyramid

The Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework categorizes NBFCs into four tiers based on size, activity, and systemic risk:

```
                          ┌─────────────┐
                          │  TOP LAYER  │  (Currently Empty; extreme systemic risk)
                       ┌──┴─────────────┴──┐
                       │    UPPER LAYER    │  (TOP 10 ELIGIBLE BY ASSET SIZE +
                    ┌──┴───────────────────┴──┐ Score-based inclusions; Bank-like rules)
                    │       MIDDLE LAYER      │  (All NBFC-D + Non-deposit ≥ ₹1,000 Cr;
                 ┌──┴─────────────────────────┴──┐ HFCs, SPDs, CICs, Infrastructure FIs)
                 │          BASE LAYER           │  (Non-deposit < ₹1,000 Cr; P2P, AA;
                 └───────────────────────────────┘  Net Owned Funds min ₹10 Cr)
```

| SBR Layer | Qualifying Criteria & Scale | Regulatory Stringency & Governance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Top Layer (NBFC-TL)** | Systemically extreme risk entities (Currently empty; populated only if RBI identifies extreme contagion/spillover risk). | Highest possible supervisory scrutiny and customized capital buffers. |
| **Upper Layer (NBFC-UL)** | • **Top 10 Eligible NBFCs by Asset Size** shall **ALWAYS be included in the Upper Layer**, irrespective of any other factor.<br>• Additional NBFCs identified based on a parametric scoring methodology (Size 35%, Interconnectedness 25%, Complexity 10%, Nature of Activity 30%). | **Bank-Like Regulations:**<br>• Mandatory **Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) of 9.0%**.<br>• Mandatory listing on stock exchange within 3 years.<br>• Standard asset provisioning aligned with banks.<br>• Mandatory Board Risk Committees, CCO, and CRO. |
| **Middle Layer (NBFC-ML)** | • **All Deposit-Taking NBFCs (NBFC-D)** irrespective of asset size.<br>• Non-Deposit taking NBFCs with **Asset Size ≥ ₹1,000 Crore**.<br>• All **Housing Finance Companies (HFCs)**, Standalone Primary Dealers (SPDs), Core Investment Companies (CICs), and Infrastructure Finance Companies (IFCs). | Standard capital adequacy (CRAR 15%), 90-day NPA classification, appointment of Chief Risk Officer (CRO). |
| **Base Layer (NBFC-BL)** | • Non-deposit taking NBFCs with **Asset Size < ₹1,000 Crore**.<br>• NBFC-Peer to Peer (P2P), NBFC-Account Aggregators (AA), and Non-Operative Financial Holding Companies (NOFHC). | Light-touch regulation; Net Owned Funds (NOF) requirement raised in phases to **₹10 Crore**. |

### 3. Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) under RBI Oversight

• **Regulatory Transfer:** Under the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019, regulatory powers over Housing Finance Companies were transferred from the **National Housing Bank (NHB) to the Reserve Bank of India** (NHB retains supervisory inspection).  
• **Principal Business Criteria for HFCs:**
  - Minimum **60% of total assets** must be deployed in providing housing finance.
  - Of this, at least **50% of total assets** must be deployed in **individual housing loans**.

### 4. Co-Lending Model (CLM 80:20)

• **Regulatory Mandate:** RBI Master Circular on Co-Lending by Banks and NBFCs to the Priority Sector.  
• **Mandatory Minimum Risk Retention:** The NBFC must retain a **minimum 20% share of each individual loan** on its balance sheet; the partner Commercial Bank takes up to **80%**.  
• **Single Blended Interest Rate:** The borrower is charged a single blended interest rate reflecting the weighted average of the bank's and NBFC's agreed cost of funds.

### 5. Bank Finance to NBFCs, Fair Practices Code & Integrated Ombudsman

• **Bank Lending to NBFCs & PSL On-Lending:** Under RBI guidelines, bank credit to registered NBFCs (other than MFIs) for on-lending is eligible for classification under Priority Sector Lending up to prescribed per-borrower caps (e.g. Agriculture up to ₹10 Lakh; Micro & Small Enterprises up to ₹20 Lakh). Under the **Large Exposure Framework (LEF)**, a bank's exposure to a single NBFC is capped at **20% of Tier 1 capital** (extendable to 25% for infrastructure financing NBFCs).  
• **NBFC Fair Practices Code (FPC):** All NBFCs must adopt a board-approved FPC requiring: (1) Written loan agreements disclosing the **all-inclusive annualized interest rate**; (2) Strict prohibition of coercive, harassing, or intimidating recovery practices; (3) Transparent notice before altering terms and conditions.  
• **Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS, 2021):** Integrates ombudsman mechanisms under a **'One Nation One Ombudsman'** framework. Extends coverage to **all Deposit-Taking NBFCs** and **Non-Deposit taking NBFCs with customer interface having asset size $\ge$ ₹100 Crore**.

---

### Examiner Trap Vault: Unit 24 & Unit 25 High-Yield Distractors

1. **Trap — Upper Layer Membership Rule:** Under RBI SBR guidelines, the **Top 10 eligible NBFCs by asset size are AUTOMATICALLY in the Upper Layer**. It is NOT the top 25 or top 50!
2. **Trap — Microfinance Income Limit:** The household annual income limit for microfinance loans is a uniform **₹3,00,000 across BOTH rural and urban areas**. An option stating ₹1.2 Lakh rural and ₹2 Lakh urban is **outdated**.

4. **Trap — DICGC Insurance on NBFC Deposits:** Public deposits held with deposit-taking NBFCs are **NOT insured by DICGC**. DICGC covers deposits with commercial and cooperative banks up to ₹5 Lakh, but **zero cover for NBFCs**.
5. **Trap — Co-Lending Risk Retention:** In the Co-Lending Model (CLM), the NBFC must retain **at least 20% risk share** on its own books.
6. **Trap — Integrated Ombudsman NBFC Threshold:** Non-deposit taking NBFCs are covered under the Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS 2021) only if they have customer interface AND an asset size of **₹100 Crore or above** (all NBFC-Ds are covered irrespective of asset size).

> **Core Proposition:** DFIs provide long-gestation project finance. India's early DFIs (IFCI, ICICI, IDBI) faced asset-liability mismatches when concessional funding ended post-1991, prompting their conversion into universal commercial banks. The DFI model was revived in 2021 through the statutory creation of NaBFID for infrastructure financing.

### 1. Historical Evolution of Indian DFIs (1948 – 2000)

| Institution | Inception Year & Statutory Basis | Original Institutional Mandate | Post-Reform Transformation & Current Status |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI)** | **1 July 1948**; IFCI Act, 1948 | **India's FIRST DFI.** Established to provide medium and long-term debt to large industrial manufacturing units. | Converted into a public limited company in 1993; currently functions as a Systemically Important Non-Deposit NBFC (NBFC-ND-SI) under Government ownership. |
| **Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India (ICICI)** | **January 1955**; Promoted by World Bank, GoI & private enterprise | Channeled foreign currency loans and equity underwriting to private sector industrial enterprises. | **Reverse Merger in 2002:** The parent DFI (ICICI) merged into its retail banking subsidiary (*ICICI Bank Ltd*), pioneering the **Universal Banking** model in India. |
| **Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI)** | **July 1964**; IDBI Act, 1964 (Apex DFI) | Established as a wholly-owned subsidiary of RBI to coordinate, refinance, and supervise all industrial DFIs; made autonomous in 1976. | **Commercial Banking Transition in 2004:** Transformed into a full-service commercial bank (*IDBI Bank Ltd*) under the IDBI (Repeal) Act, 2003; LIC acquired majority stake in 2019. |
| **Unit Trust of India (UTI)** | **1964**; UTI Act, 1963 | Pioneer mutual fund mobilizing retail savings for industrial equities; managed the historic US-64 scheme. | Bifurcated in 2002 into **SUUTI** (holding government legacy assets) and **UTI Mutual Fund** (SEBI-registered mutual fund). |

---

### 2. The Universal Banking Transition (Khan & Narasimham Committees)

• **The ALM Crisis of DFIs:** Pre-1991, DFIs received subsidized, low-cost long-term funding through the RBI's **National Industrial Credit (Long Term Operations) - NIC-LTO funds** and government-guaranteed bonds. In the post-reform era, these concessional windows ceased. DFIs were forced to borrow at market interest rates via 3–5 year bonds to fund 15–20 year industrial infrastructure loans, triggering acute **Asset-Liability Mismatch (ALM)**.  
• **The Solution (Universal Banking):** The **Khan Committee (1998)** and **Narasimham Committee II (1998)** recommended phasing out specialized DFIs in favor of **Universal Banks**—institutions offering under a single corporate umbrella the full continuum of commercial banking, investment banking, long-term project finance, and asset management.

---

### 3. Specialized All-India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)

| Institution | Establishment Year & Statute | Apex Refinancing Role | Ownership Pattern |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **NABARD** | **12 July 1982**; NABARD Act, 1981 (B. Sivaraman Committee) | Apex refinance institution for **Agriculture, Rural Development, RRBs, and Rural Cooperative Banks**. Administers the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF). | **100% Government of India** (RBI divested its remaining stake in 2019). |
| **EXIM Bank** | **1982**; Export-Import Bank of India Act, 1981 | Apex institution for financing, facilitating, and promoting **India's international merchandise and services trade**. Extends Lines of Credit (LOC) to foreign sovereigns. | **100% Government of India**. |
| **National Housing Bank (NHB)** | **9 July 1988**; National Housing Bank Act, 1987 | Apex refinance institution for **Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) and mortgage lenders**. Supervises HFCs (while RBI exercises regulatory control). | **100% Government of India** (Transferred from RBI in 2019). |
| **SIDBI** | **2 April 1990**; SIDBI Act, 1989 | Principal financial institution for promotion, financing, and refinancing of the **Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise (MSME) sector**. Co-promoter of CGTMSE. | Institutional shareholding (SBI, LIC, public sector banks, and GoI). |

---

### 4. Modern DFI Revival: NaBFID (Act 2021)

• **Establishment:** Set up under the **National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development Act, 2021** as a specialized statutory DFI to fund the National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP).  
• **Capital Structure:**
  - Authorized Share Capital: **₹1,00,000 Crore**.
  - Initial Paid-Up Capital: **₹20,000 Crore** (Government of India holds minimum 26% equity).
  - Initial Sovereign Grant: **₹5,000 Crore** provided by the Central Government.
• **Regulatory Mandate:** Regulated and supervised by the RBI as the **Fifth All-India Financial Institution (AIFI)** under Sections 45L and 45N of the RBI Act, 1934.  
• **Dual Objective:** (1) Financial objective: Direct lending, syndication, and refinancing of infrastructure projects; (2) Developmental objective: Deepening the domestic long-term corporate debt and derivatives market for infrastructure.

> **Core Proposition:** Financial inclusion integrates unbanked segments via PMJDY, measured by the RBI FI-Index. Digital public infrastructure managed by NPCI and the introduction of the Digital Rupee (CBDC) underpin modern retail banking rails.

### 1. Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY)

• **Core Mandate:** National Mission for Financial Inclusion launched on **28 August 2014**.  
• **Key Financial Inclusion Features:**
  - Universal access to basic banking services via **Basic Savings Bank Deposit Accounts (BSBDA)** with zero minimum balance requirement.
  - **Overdraft (OD) Facility:** Up to **₹10,000** to eligible account holders (one per household, preferably woman of house; no conditions attached for OD up to ₹2,000; age bracket: **18 to 65 years**).
  - **RuPay Debit Card:** Includes an inbuilt **Accidental Insurance Cover of ₹2 Lakh** (for accounts opened after 28 August 2018).

### 2. The RBI Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index)

Introduced by the RBI in **August 2021** to measure the extent of financial inclusion across the country:
• **Scoring Metric:** A single value ranging between **0 and 100**, where **0 represents complete financial exclusion** and **100 represents complete financial inclusion**.  
• **Three Dimensional Weights:**
  $$\text{FI-Index} = \mathbf{Access (35\%)} + \mathbf{Usage (45\%)} + \mathbf{Quality (20\%)} = 100\%$$
• **Unique Design Property:** Calculated annually in July **without a base year**, reflecting cumulative historical achievements across banking, investments, insurance, and postal services.

### 3. Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC / Digital Rupee - e₹)

• **Statutory Basis:** Enabled via amendments to Section 22 and Section 2 of the RBI Act, 1934, passed under the **Finance Act, 2022**, recognizing CBDC as sovereign legal tender currency.  
• **Key Design Dimensions:**
  - **Wholesale CBDC ($e₹-W$):** Launched November 2022; restricted to institutional interbank settlement of secondary market transactions in Government Securities.
  - **Retail CBDC ($e₹-R$):** Launched December 2022; digital token representing sovereign currency issued to retail users via authorized bank digital wallets for peer-to-peer (P2P) and peer-to-merchant (P2M) payments.
  - **Interest-Free Nature:** To prevent disintermediation of commercial bank deposits, **the Digital Rupee earns ZERO interest**.

6. **Trap — Interest on CBDC:** The Reserve Bank of India pays **ZERO interest on CBDC (Digital Rupee)** balances to protect commercial bank deposits from flight to central bank currency.

> **Core Proposition:** Financial markets are segmented by instrument maturity into Money Markets (maturity ≤ 1 year, liquidity management under RBI) and Capital Markets (maturity > 1 year, long-term capital formation under SEBI), operating across primary and secondary trading venues.

### 1. Money Market vs. Capital Market Master Matrix

| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| **Primary Statutory Regulator** | **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** | **Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)** |

---46:T2975,> **Curriculum Alignment — Official IIBF Paper 1 Benchmark (Unit 30)**  
> **Core Proposition:** Money market instruments provide short-term liquidity management for banks, the sovereign, and corporate borrowers. Under RBI directions, both Commercial Paper (CP) and Certificates of Deposit (CD) carry a minimum denomination of ₹5 Lakh.

### 1. Call, Notice & Term Money Market

• **Call Money:** Interbank borrowing or lending for **Overnight (1 Day)** to address immediate reserve (CRR) mismatches.  
• **Notice Money:** Interbank borrowing or lending for **2 Days up to 14 Days**.  
• **Term Money:** Interbank borrowing or lending for **15 Days up to 1 Year (365 Days)** without collateral.  
• **Eligible Participants:** Scheduled Commercial Banks, Payment Banks, Small Finance Banks, Cooperative Banks, and Primary Dealers (PDs). Non-bank institutions (corporates, mutual funds) are **prohibited from lending/borrowing** in the uncollateralized call/notice market.

---

### 2. Treasury Bills (T-Bills) & Cash Management Bills (CMBs)

• **Issuing Authority:** Issued by the Reserve Bank of India on behalf of the Central Government.  
• **Issuance Nature:** Issued at a **discount to face value and redeemed at par (₹100)**; carry zero coupon interest.  
• **Tenors & Auction Schedule (Current RBI Auction Calendar):**
  - **91-Day T-Bills:** Weekly auction (every Wednesday).
  - **182-Day T-Bills:** Weekly auction (every Wednesday).
  - **364-Day T-Bills:** Weekly auction (every Wednesday).
• **Minimum Denomination:** Multiples of **₹10,000**. Eligible for SLR maintenance by commercial banks.  
• **Cash Management Bills (CMBs):** Short-term non-standardized zero-coupon bills issued to meet temporary cash flow mismatches of the Central Government for **maturities of less than 91 days**.

---

### 3. Commercial Paper (CP) vs. Certificates of Deposit (CD)

| Parameter | Commercial Paper (CP) | Certificates of Deposit (CD) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Instrument Character** | Unsecured promissory note issued by corporate borrowers | Negotiable, transferable promissory note issued against bank term deposits |
| **Eligible Issuers** | Highly rated Corporates, Primary Dealers (PDs), All-India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) | **Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs)** and select All-India Financial Institutions |
| **Minimum Denomination** | **₹5 Lakh** (and in multiples of ₹5 Lakh thereafter) | **₹5 Lakh** (and in multiples of ₹5 Lakh thereafter) (*Current RBI Master Direction*) |
| **Maturity / Tenor Range** | **Minimum 7 Days up to Maximum 1 Year** | • **Issued by Banks:** **Min 7 Days to Max 1 Year**<br>• **Issued by FIs:** **Min 1 Year to Max 3 Years** |
| **Credit Rating Mandate** | Minimum rating of **A3** (or equivalent) by SEBI-registered CRA | Rating mandatory if issued by FIs; banks issue based on board policy |
| **Loans Against Instrument** | **Strictly PROHIBITED** (Banks cannot grant loans against CP) | **Strictly PROHIBITED** (Banks cannot grant loans against their own CDs) |
| **Secondary Market Trading** | Dematerialized format (FBIL benchmark reference / FIMMDA conventions) | Dematerialized format; transferable by delivery and endorsement |

> **Critical Regulatory Update — CD Minimum Denomination:**  
> Under the RBI's Master Direction on Certificates of Deposit, the minimum denomination of a CD is **₹5 Lakh and in multiples of ₹5 Lakh thereafter** (identical to Commercial Paper). An option citing ₹1 Lakh is **outdated and invalid**.

---

### 4. Triparty Repo (TREPS)

• **Mechanism:** A repurchase agreement where a third party—the **Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL)**—acts as an intermediary to provide collateral valuation, allocation, and settlement services.  
• **Risk Mitigation:** CCIL acts as the **Central Counterparty (CCP)**, executing multilateral netting and trade novation. This **mitigates counterparty credit risk** across interbank repo trades, enabling non-bank entities (Mutual Funds, Insurance companies) to participate in overnight secured lending.

---

### 5. Bills Rediscounting Scheme (BRDS)

• **Origin & Historical Basis:** Introduced by the RBI in **November 1970** following the recommendations of the Narasimham Working Group (Study Group on the Bill Market Scheme) to foster a genuine, liquid commercial trade bill market in India.  
• **Operational Mechanism:**
  1. A seller draws a bill of exchange on the buyer against a genuine domestic trade sale of goods; the buyer accepts the bill.
  2. The seller discounts the trade bill with their commercial bank.
  3. Under BRDS, the discounting bank, to manage short-term liquidity, **rediscounts the eligible commercial bill** with the RBI or approved institutional rediscounting agencies (LIC, GIC, UTI, other commercial banks).
• **Statutory Eligibility Rules:**
  - Must be a **genuine trade bill** arising from the actual physical sale and delivery of goods. **Accommodation bills (kite-flying finance bills) are strictly prohibited**.
  - Must carry at least **two good signatures** (the drawer/seller and the drawee/buyer or an accepting bank).
  - Original tenor of the underlying trade bill cannot exceed **180 days**, while the rediscounting maturity is typically capped at **90 days**.

---

### 6. Long-Term Repo Operations (LTRO & TLTRO)

• **Institutional Purpose:** Introduced by the RBI in **February 2020** as a specialized liquidity injection tool to transmit policy rate cuts directly into corporate borrowing costs when money market spreads widen during stress periods.  
• **Mechanics:**
  - Unlike standard Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) repos which operate overnight or for 7/14-day tenors, LTRO provides banks with durable central bank liquidity for **tenors of 1 year and 3 years at the prevailing policy repo rate**.
  - Banks place Government Securities as collateral and receive term liquidity at a fixed, low borrowing cost.
• **Targeted Long-Term Repo Operations (TLTRO):**
  - Launched during the March 2020 pandemic economic shock.
  - Specified tranches (e.g. TLTRO 1.0, TLTRO 2.0) required borrowing banks to deploy the liquidity into **investment-grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and non-convertible debentures** of targeted sectors (especially NBFCs, MFIs, and HFCs), successfully reviving corporate debt liquidity.

---

### Examiner Trap Vault: Unit 29 & Unit 30 High-Yield Distractors

1. **Trap — CD vs CP Minimum Denomination:** Both Commercial Paper (CP) and Certificates of Deposit (CD) have the **exact same minimum denomination of ₹5 Lakh and in multiples of ₹5 Lakh thereafter**. Do NOT choose ₹1 Lakh for CD.
2. **Trap — Bank Loans Against CD/CP:** Banks are **STRICTLY PROHIBITED from granting loans or advances against their own CDs or against CPs**.
3. **Trap — Call vs Notice vs Term Tenors:** Call Money is **1 day (overnight)**; Notice Money is **2 to 14 days**; Term Money is **15 to 365 days**.
4. **Trap — TREPS Counterparty Risk:** TREPS does not eliminate all systemic risk through magic; it **mitigates counterparty credit risk through CCP multilateral netting and novation by CCIL**.
5. **Trap — BRDS Bill Eligibility:** An accommodation bill (a bill drawn without an underlying commercial trade transaction to raise finance) is **strictly ineligible for rediscounting under BRDS**. Only genuine commercial trade bills qualify.
6. **Trap — LTRO Tenor:** LTROs operate for **1-year and 3-year tenors**, not standard 14-day repo tenors.

| Capital Issue Type | Statutory Definition | Target Investor Base & Rules |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Initial Public Offering (IPO)** | An unlisted company offering fresh equity shares or an Offer for Sale to the public for the first time. | Retail Individual Investors (RII), Non-Institutional Investors (NII), Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIB). |
| **Follow-on Public Offering (FPO)** | An already listed company issuing additional fresh equity shares to the public. | General public and institutions. |
| **Rights Issue** | An issue of shares offered to **existing shareholders** in proportion to their existing holding as on a record date. | Existing shareholders; rights entitlements can be renounced in favor of third parties. |
| **Bonus Issue** | Capitalization of free reserves into fully paid-up additional shares issued free of cost to existing shareholders. | Existing equity holders; share capital expands while net worth remains unchanged. |
| **Qualified Institutional Placement (QIP)** | Private placement of equity shares or convertible securities by a listed company to **Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs)**. | Fast-track institutional route allotted exclusively to **Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIBs)** as defined under SEBI ICDR Regulations (illustrative eligible categories include Mutual Funds, Insurance Companies, registered FPIs, Scheduled Commercial Banks, AIFs, and Pension Funds); retail investors are not eligible. |
| **Offer for Sale (OFS)** | Fast-track bidding window on the stock exchange for promoters or large shareholders to dilute equity holdings. | General public and institutions to comply with minimum 25% public shareholding norms. |

• **Applications Supported by Blocked Amount (ASBA):** Prescribed blocked-funds mechanism for relevant public issue categories (IPOs/FPOs) and designated rights issues. The application funds **remain in the investor's own bank account (lien marked)** via Self-Certified Syndicate Banks (SCSBs), continuing to earn interest, and are debited only upon successful allotment of shares.  
• **T+1 Rolling Settlement:** India was the first major global economy to transition 100% of equity trades to **T+1 rolling settlement** (trades settle within 24 hours).

> **Core Proposition:** Fixed income markets establish the sovereign yield curve through G-Secs, SDLs, and SGBs. Yield-to-Maturity and Duration govern interest rate risk, valued under official **FBIL benchmark curves** alongside **FIMMDA market conventions**. Retail participation is enabled via the RBI Retail Direct Scheme, while corporate short-term funding includes Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs).

### 1. Sovereign Debt Instruments: G-Secs, SDLs & SGBs

| Instrument | Issuing Authority & Backing | Key Tenor & Coupon Properties |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Central G-Secs (Dated Securities)** | Issued by RBI on behalf of the Central Government | Semi-annual fixed coupon; maturities up to 40–50 years; zero credit default risk; 100% SLR eligible. |
| **State Development Loans (SDLs)** | Issued by RBI on behalf of 28 State Governments | Semi-annual interest; yields typically **30–60 bps higher than Central G-Secs**; eligible for SLR maintenance. |
| **Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs)** | Issued by RBI on behalf of the Central Government | Denominated in grams of gold (min 1g; max 4kg individual); Tenor **8 years with exit option after 5th year**; **Fixed interest rate of 2.50% p.a.** paid semi-annually (fully taxable); **Capital gains tax exempt** on redemption at maturity (*Note: Effective from 1 April 2026 under amended tax provisions, this exemption applies strictly to an individual subscriber who acquired the bond through original subscription and held it continuously until maturity; secondary market purchases redeemed at maturity are taxable as capital gains*). |

---

### 2. Bond Valuation, Yield to Maturity & Duration Formulas

$$\text{Dirty Price} = \text{Clean Price} + \text{Accrued Interest}$$

$$\text{Accrued Interest} = \text{Coupon Amount} \times \left( \frac{\text{Days elapsed since last coupon}}{\text{Total days in coupon period}} \right)$$

• **Yield to Maturity (YTM):** The internal rate of return (IRR) of a bond, equating the present value of all future coupon cash flows and principal redemption to the current market price of the bond.  
• **Inverse Price-Yield Relationship:** When market interest rates rise, bond prices **fall**; when market interest rates fall, bond prices **rise**.  
• **Macaulay Duration ($D_{\text{mac}}$):** The weighted average maturity of the cash flows of a bond:
  $$D_{\text{mac}} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^n \frac{t \cdot C_t}{(1+y)^t}}{\text{Current Bond Market Price}}$$
  *Crucial Rule:* For a **Zero-Coupon Bond, Macaulay Duration is EXACTLY equal to its maturity period**!  
• **Modified Duration ($D_{\text{mod}}$):** Measures the percentage price sensitivity of a bond to a 100 bps (1%) change in yield:
  $$D_{\text{mod}} = \frac{D_{\text{mac}}}{1 + \frac{y}{m}} \implies \frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx - D_{\text{mod}} \times \Delta y$$

---

### 3. Official Valuation Benchmark Administrator: FBIL & FIMMDA

• **Financial Benchmarks India Private Limited (FBIL):**  
  - Formed in **December 2014** (jointly promoted by FIMMDA, FEDAI, and IBA) as an independent benchmark administrator under RBI regulations.
  - **Sovereign Valuation Mandate:** Effective **31 March 2018**, the RBI formally mandated that **FBIL assumed full responsibility for administering and publishing daily benchmark valuation curves for Government Securities (Central G-Secs, T-Bills, and SDLs)**. FIMMDA ceased publishing independent G-Sec valuation prices on that date.
  - FBIL also publishes overnight call benchmarks (MIBOR), treasury bill rates, and reference exchange rates.
• **Fixed Income Money Market and Derivatives Association of India (FIMMDA):**  
  - Established in **May 1998** as a **Self-Regulatory Organization (SRO)** representing SCBs, All-India Financial Institutions, Primary Dealers, and Insurance Companies.
  - Formulates standardized market trading conventions, operational documentation, and codes of conduct.
  - In fixed-income valuation, FIMMDA collaborates with FBIL and continues to publish the **daily corporate bond valuation matrix / credit spreads** used by institutional portfolios.

---

### 4. RBI Retail Direct Scheme

• **Launch:** Introduced by the RBI in **November 2021** to democratize retail investor access to the sovereign government debt market.  
• **Retail Direct Gilt (RDG) Account:** Individual retail investors can open a dedicated **RDG Account online directly with the RBI**.  
• **Zero Charges:** **Zero account opening fees and zero account maintenance charges**.  
• **Investment Access:**
  - *Primary Market:* Direct non-competitive bidding participation in primary auctions of Central G-Secs, Treasury Bills, SDLs, and Sovereign Gold Bonds.
  - *Secondary Market:* Seamless secondary market trading via integration with the RBI's screen-based **NDS-OM (Negotiated Dealing System - Order Matching)** platform.

---

### 5. Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs)

• **Definition:** Unsecured short-term borrowing and lending arrangements executed directly between two corporate entities.  
• **Governing Statute:** Regulated under **Section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013** (Loans and investments by companies).  
• **Regulatory Exemptions:** Exempt from SEBI regulations (since it is a bilateral transaction between corporate entities) and exempt from RBI banking regulation provided the lending entity is not registered as an NBFC.  
• **Risk & Pricing:** Completely unsecured; carries higher credit default risk than bank term deposits, commanding higher interest rates.  
• **Operational Tenor Categories:**
  1. **3-Month ICDs:** The most common market instrument, utilized by cash-rich corporates to earn short-term returns on idle treasury cash.
  2. **6-Month ICDs:** Extended for medium short-term corporate liquidity needs.
  3. **Call ICDs:** Repayable upon **1 day's notice** by the lending corporation.

### Examiner Trap Vault: Unit 31 & Unit 32 High-Yield Distractors

1. **Trap — Zero-Coupon Bond Duration:** The Macaulay Duration of a Zero-Coupon Bond **EQUALS its maturity period** (e.g., a 5-year zero-coupon bond has a duration of exactly 5 years).
2. **Trap — SGB Tenor, Coupon & 2026 Tax Condition:** Sovereign Gold Bonds carry a **fixed interest rate of 2.50% p.a.** paid semi-annually (fully taxable), with a **tenor of 8 years (exit option after 5th year)**. Exemption from capital gains tax at maturity redemption from 1 April 2026 applies **strictly to original individual subscribers held continuously to maturity**.
3. **Trap — G-Sec Valuation Administrator (FBIL vs FIMMDA):** Since **31 March 2018, FBIL (Financial Benchmarks India Pvt Ltd)** is the official benchmark administrator publishing daily G-Sec, SDL, and T-Bill valuation curves under RBI directions. FIMMDA is an industry SRO publishing corporate bond spreads.
4. **Trap — RBI Retail Direct Costs:** Opening and maintaining an RDG account under the RBI Retail Direct Scheme is **completely free of cost (Zero fees)**.
5. **Trap — Governing Law for ICDs:** Inter-Corporate Deposits are governed under **Section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013**, NOT the RBI Act or SEBI Act.
6. **Trap — ASBA Fund Retention:** In an ASBA application, money is **never transferred to the issuer company** at the time of bidding; it remains blocked in the investor's own bank account.

> **Core Proposition:** The Indian foreign exchange market operates under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, regulated by the RBI with market conventions established by FEDAI. Cross-border capital is channeled through specialized NRI deposit accounts (NRE, NRO, FCNR(B)).

### 1. Market Infrastructure & Exchange Quotation Conventions

• **Foreign Exchange Dealers' Association of India (FEDAI):** Established in **1958**; self-regulatory body formulating market conventions, uniform rules, and codes of conduct for Authorized Dealer banks in India.  
• **Authorized Persons (FEMA Categorization):**
  - *Authorized Dealer Category-I (AD Cat-I):* Commercial banks authorized to handle all current and capital account transactions.
  - *Authorized Dealer Category-II (AD Cat-II):* Upgraded money changers authorized to handle non-trade related personal remittances.
  - *Authorized Dealer Category-III (AD Cat-III):* Select financial institutions handling specific foreign exchange transactions.
• **Exchange Rate Quotations:**
  - *Direct Quotation:* Units of domestic currency per unit of foreign currency (e.g. $1\text{ USD} = ₹85.00$). In India, **all foreign exchange quotations are given as Direct Quotes** since 2 August 1993.
  - *Indirect Quotation:* Units of foreign currency per unit of domestic currency (e.g. $₹100 = 1.18\text{ USD}$).
• **Value Dates (Foreign Exchange Settlement):**
  - **Cash / Ready:** Settlement of funds on the **same day of the transaction ($T$)**.
  - **TOM (Tomorrow):** Settlement on the **next business day ($T+1$)**.
  - **SPOT:** Settlement on the **second working business day ($T+2$)** following the transaction date. Spot rate is the primary benchmark rate.
  - **FORWARD:** Settlement on any agreed date **beyond the Spot date ($> T+2$)**.

### 2. NRI Bank Accounts: Comprehensive Master Comparison Matrix

| Regulatory Parameter | Non-Resident External (NRE) Account | Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) Account | Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR-B) Account |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Permitted Currency** | **Indian Rupees (INR)** | **Indian Rupees (INR)** | **Designated Foreign Currencies** (USD, GBP, EUR, JPY, AUD, CAD) |
| **Permitted Account Types** | Savings, Current, Recurring, Fixed Deposit | Savings, Current, Recurring, Fixed Deposit | **Term / Fixed Deposit ONLY** (No Savings/Current accounts!) |
| **Permitted Deposit Source** | Inward remittances from abroad in foreign exchange, or transfers from another NRE/FCNR account. | Inward remittances AND **legitimate local Indian earnings** (rent, dividends, pension). | Inward remittances in designated foreign currency. |
| **Repatriability of Funds** | **100% Freely and Fully Repatriable** (Principal and interest can be sent abroad freely). | **Restricted Repatriability:** Current income is repatriable; capital is capped at **$1 Million USD per financial year** (with tax certificate Form 15CA/15CB). | **100% Freely and Fully Repatriable** (Principal and interest can be remitted overseas). |
| **Foreign Exchange Risk** | Borne by the **Depositor / NRI** (Currency converted to INR on deposit and converted back on withdrawal). | Borne by the **Depositor / NRI**. | Borne entirely by the **Bank**! The depositor faces **ZERO foreign exchange risk**. |
| **Indian Income Tax Status** | **Completely Tax-Free** (Interest earned is 100% exempt under Section 10(4)(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961). | **Taxable:** Subject to applicable **TDS (Tax Deducted at Source)** (typically 30% plus surcharge/cess, or lower withholding rates under applicable DTAA). | **Completely Tax-Free** (Interest earned is 100% exempt under Section 10(15)(iv)(fa) of the Income-tax Act). |
| **Permitted Tenor Range** | Term deposits: Minimum **1 Year** up to Maximum **10 Years**. | Standard bank term deposit tenors (7 days up to 10 years). | **Minimum 1 Year up to Maximum 5 Years**. |
| **Joint Account Holding** | Permitted jointly with other NRIs, or with resident Indian relative on **'Former or Survivor' basis**. | Permitted jointly with other NRIs or resident Indian relatives. | Permitted with other NRIs, or with resident relative on **'Former or Survivor' basis**. |

### 3. FEMA 1999 vs. FERA 1973

• **Legislative Shift:** The Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999 replaced the draconian Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA), 1973 with effect from **1 June 2000**.  
• **Decriminalization:** Violations under FERA were treated as **criminal offenses** with imprisonment. Violations under FEMA are treated as **civil infractions** remediable by monetary penalties, with compounding provisions administered by the RBI and the Directorate of Enforcement (ED).

### 4. FX-Retail Platform & CCIL Infrastructure

• **FX-Retail Platform:** Rolled out by the **Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL)** under RBI direction to deliver transparent, competitive, and order-driven real-time foreign exchange pricing directly to retail customers (individuals, MSMEs) executing transactions through Authorized Dealer Category-I banks.  
• **Settlement Guarantee:** CCIL acts as the Central Counterparty (CCP), mitigating settlement risk through multilateral netting and guaranteed delivery versus payment settlement.

### 5. LIBOR Cessation & Alternative Reference Rates (ARRs)

The cessation of the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) prompted a global transition to transaction-based **Alternative Reference Rates (ARRs)** based on overnight risk-free rates (RFRs):

| Currency | Benchmark Alternative Reference Rate (ARR) | Administering Sovereign Authority | Rate Nature |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **USD** | **SOFR** (Secured Overnight Financing Rate) | Federal Reserve Bank of New York | Secured overnight repo rate |
| **GBP** | **SONIA** (Sterling Overnight Index Average) | Bank of England | Unsecured overnight rate |
| **JPY** | **TONAR** (Tokyo Overnight Average Rate) | Bank of Japan | Unsecured overnight call rate |
| **EUR** | **€STR** (Euro Short-Term Rate) | European Central Bank (ECB) | Wholesale unsecured overnight rate |
| **INR** | **Modified MIFOR** (replaces USD LIBOR-linked MIFOR) | Financial Benchmarks India Pvt Ltd (FBIL) | SOFR + domestic forex swap spread |

### 6. US Dollar Index (USDX) Basket & ADR / GDR Mechanisms

• **US Dollar Index (USDX) Basket:** Measures the purchasing power of the US Dollar against a geometric trade-weighted basket of six major international currencies:  
  $$\text{Euro (EUR): } \mathbf{57.6\%} \quad\Big|\quad \text{Japanese Yen (JPY): } \mathbf{13.6\%} \quad\Big|\quad \text{Pound Sterling (GBP): } \mathbf{11.9\%}$$  
  $$\text{Canadian Dollar (CAD): } \mathbf{9.1\%} \quad\Big|\quad \text{Swedish Krona (SEK): } \mathbf{4.2\%} \quad\Big|\quad \text{Swiss Franc (CHF): } \mathbf{3.6\%}$$  
• **ADR / GDR Two-Way Fungibility:**  
  - **American Depository Receipts (ADRs):** Negotiable USD-denominated instruments issued by a US depository bank representing shares of non-US companies traded on US exchanges (NYSE, NASDAQ).  
  - **Global Depository Receipts (GDRs):** Depository receipts traded outside the US (e.g. London, Luxembourg). Under SEBI/RBI regulations, **Two-Way Fungibility** permits investors to convert domestic Indian shares into depository receipts and reconvert DRs back into local shares within foreign investment limits.

> **Core Proposition:** Derivatives derive value from underlying assets. Market structures span OTC contracts (Forwards, Swaps, CDS) and exchange-traded standardized contracts (Futures, Options). Risk exposures are quantified via Option Greeks and governed by ISDA documentation.

### 1. Forwards vs. Futures Contracts

| Dimension | Forward Contracts | Futures Contracts |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Trading Venue** | Over-the-Counter (OTC) private bilateral market | Organized national exchanges (NSE, BSE, MCX) |
| **Contract Specifications** | **Customized** (Non-standardized amounts and settlement dates) | **Standardized** (Fixed contract size, expiration cycle) |
| **Counterparty Credit Risk** | High counterparty default risk (Bilateral settlement) | **Near zero**; guaranteed by exchange Clearing Corporation |
| **Settlement Mechanism** | Typically settled on maturity by physical delivery | Settled daily via **Mark-to-Market (MTM) Margin calls** |

---

### 2. Options Architecture & Option Greeks

An **Option** confers the right, but not the obligation, to buy (**Call Option**) or sell (**Put Option**) an underlying asset at a specified Strike Price ($K$) on or before expiration.

| Option Greek | Mathematical Partial Derivative | Financial Meaning & Interpretation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Delta ($\Delta$)** | $$\Delta = \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}$$ | Measures the sensitivity of the option price ($V$) to a ₹1 change in the underlying asset price ($S$). Call Delta ranges between **0 and +1**; Put Delta ranges between **-1 and 0**. |
| **Gamma ($\Gamma$)** | $$\Gamma = \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2} = \frac{\partial \Delta}{\partial S}$$ | Measures the rate of change of Delta for a change in underlying price. Quantifies the curvature of the option price profile. |
| **Theta ($\Theta$)** | $$\Theta = \frac{\partial V}{\partial t}$$ | Measures **Time Decay**—the rate at which an option loses value as expiration approaches. Almost always negative for long option holders. |
| **Vega ($\nu$)** | $$\nu = \frac{\partial V}{\partial \sigma}$$ | Measures the sensitivity of the option price to a 1% change in the **implied volatility** ($\sigma$) of the underlying asset. |
| **Rho ($\rho$)** | $$\rho = \frac{\partial V}{\partial r}$$ | Measures the sensitivity of the option price to a change in the risk-free interest rate ($r$). |

---

### 3. Credit Default Swaps (CDS)

• **Mechanism:** A bilateral OTC contract where the **Protection Buyer** pays periodic premium fees to the **Protection Seller**. In return, if a defined **Credit Event** (Bankruptcy, Failure to Pay, Obligation Default, Debt Restructuring) occurs regarding the debt issuer (**Reference Entity**), the protection seller pays compensation (cash or physical delivery of defaulted bonds) to make the buyer whole.  
• **Documentation:** Transacted under the standardized **International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) Master Agreement**.  
• **RBI CDS Directions:** Commercial banks can act as Protection Buyers to hedge their credit exposures on corporate bonds. Capital adequacy charges must be maintained by protection sellers.

### Examiner Trap Vault: Unit 33 & Unit 36 High-Yield Distractors

1. **Trap — NRE vs NRO Tax Treatment:** Interest earned on **NRE accounts is 100% EXEMPT from Indian income tax**, whereas interest on **NRO accounts is TAXABLE (subject to applicable TDS / DTAA rates)**.
2. **Trap — FCNR(B) Foreign Exchange Risk:** The depositor bears **ZERO exchange risk** in an FCNR(B) account because deposits and withdrawals are denominated in foreign currency; the commercial bank bears the currency risk.
3. **Trap — FCNR(B) Account Types:** FCNR(B) accounts can ONLY be opened as **Term / Fixed Deposits** (Minimum 1 year to Maximum 5 years). An option stating savings accounts are permitted in FCNR(B) is **false**.
4. **Trap — Spot Settlement Day:** Foreign exchange Spot transactions settle on the **second working business day ($T+2$)**, not next day ($T+1$).
5. **Trap — Option Delta Boundaries:** Call option Delta is bounded strictly between **0 and +1**; Put option Delta is bounded between **-1 and 0**. Delta of a deep in-the-money call approaches +1.
6. **Trap — USD Alternative Reference Rate (ARR):** The official benchmark ARR replacing USD LIBOR is **SOFR** (Secured Overnight Financing Rate, administered by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York). In India, FBIL publishes **Modified MIFOR** benchmarked to SOFR.
7. **Trap — USDX Weight Dominance:** In the US Dollar Index (USDX) basket, the **Euro (EUR)** holds the highest weight at **57.6%** (more than half the aggregate index weight).

> **Core Proposition:** Financial market integration enables rapid capital mobility and interest rate parity, but exposes the economy to systemic contagion. Commercial banks manage cross-market exposures via Integrated Treasury desks under Asset-Liability Committee (ALCO) oversight.

### 1. Levels of Financial Market Integration

| Degree of Integration | Market Characteristics & Capital Mobility | Price Discrepancies & Arbitrage |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Segmented / Low Integration** | Strict capital controls, fragmented regulatory silos, information delays, limited cross-border participant access. | Large, persistent price and yield discrepancies across markets. Arbitrage is constrained. |
| **Partially Integrated** | Emerging markets with capital account restrictions (e.g. India under FEMA). | Short-term money and forex markets exhibit strong links, while equity and bond markets experience policy-dampened transmission. |
| **Fully / Highly Integrated** | Unrestricted capital mobility, electronic straight-through processing (STP), transparent price discovery. | Price differentials disappear almost instantaneously via arbitrage. Strong law of one price holds. |

```

│                   FINANCIAL MARKET TRANSMISSION CHANNELS                    │
├─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
