└─────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

### 3. Integrated Bank Treasury Operations

In modern commercial banking, the **Integrated Treasury** consolidates domestic and foreign currency liquidity management into a unified operations center:
• **Four Core Functional Desks:**
  1. *Domestic Money Market Desk:* Manages daily reserve obligations (CRR with RBI, SLR), Call/Notice money borrowing, issuance of CDs, and TREPS operations.
  2. *Forex Treasury Desk:* Manages cross-border currency flows, covers merchant forex risk, quotes spot/forward rates, and executes currency swaps.
  3. *Investment / G-Sec Desk:* Manages sovereign bond trading, corporate bonds, commercial paper, and statutory SLR investments categorized into HTM (Held to Maturity), AFS (Available for Sale), and HFT (Held for Trading).
  4. *Derivatives Desk:* Structures and trades Interest Rate Swaps (IRS), Forward Rate Agreements (FRAs), and currency options for balance-sheet hedging.
• **Organizational Governance:**
  - **Front Office:** Dealing room executing market trades.
  - **Mid Office:** Independent risk management unit monitoring Value at Risk (VaR), stop-loss limits, counterparty exposure limits, and ALM mismatches. Reports directly to the **Chief Risk Officer (CRO)**.
  - **Back Office:** Confirmation, settlement, accounting, and regulatory reporting to RBI.
  - **Asset-Liability Committee (ALCO):** Senior management operational committee chaired by the CEO/CMD (or Executive Director) that manages asset-liability mismatches, liquidity buffers, and interest rate risk, reporting functionally to the Board's Risk Management Committee (RMC).

---

### 4. Financial Contagion & Systemic Transmission Mechanisms

**Financial Contagion** refers to the rapid cross-border or cross-institutional transmission of liquidity or solvency shocks:
• **Core Contagion Channels:**
  1. *Direct Bilateral Counterparty Exposure:* Insolvent institution defaults on interbank loans, repos, or derivative contracts, triggering cascading counterparty failures.
  2. *Fire-Sale Externality / Common Asset Exposure:* Distressed institutions dump liquid assets (G-Secs, high-grade bonds) onto the market to raise emergency cash. Collapsing asset prices force other sound banks to record heavy mark-to-market (MTM) losses, depleting regulatory capital.
  3. *Information Asymmetry / Panic Contagion:* Creditors unable to distinguish sound banks from distressed banks execute preemptive runs on all institutions sharing similar business profiles.
  4. *The Sovereign-Bank Nexus ("Doom Loop"):* Commercial banks hold large portfolios of domestic government debt. Sovereign fiscal distress reduces bond values, eroding bank capital; distressed banks then require sovereign capital bailouts, compounding the sovereign crisis.
• **Macroprudential Mitigants:** Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB), Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), and the RBI Large Exposure Framework (capping exposure to a single counterparty at 20% of Tier 1 capital, extendable to 25% for connected groups).

### 5. Asian Clearing Union (ACU) Architecture

• **Establishment & Institutional Headquarters:** Established in **1974** at the initiative of the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (**UN-ESCAP**). The permanent Secretariat and headquarters is located in **Tehran, Iran**.  
• **Member Central Banks:** Central banks of India (RBI), Bangladesh, Bhutan, Iran, Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka.  
• **Settlement Mechanism & Units:** Provides a multilateral clearing arrangement for settling payments on eligible intra-regional trade transactions among participants on a net basis, conserving foreign exchange. Transacted in **ACU Dollar** (equivalent to USD), **ACU Euro**, and **ACU JPY**. Commercial transactions are routed via Authorized Dealer Category-I banks with final net settlement executed through member central banks.

### 1. Commercial Banking vs. Merchant Banking

| Parameter | Commercial Banking | Merchant Banking |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

### 2. SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations (2026 Dual-Category Regime)

The SEBI (Merchant Bankers) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025 (effective 3 January 2026) streamlined the registration architecture by abolishing Categories III and IV, instituting a robust two-tier structure:

| Category | Permissible Scope of Activities | Mandatory Minimum Net Worth | Mandatory Liquid Net Worth |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Category I** | • Can act as **Lead Manager to Public Issues (IPOs / FPOs / Rights)**.<br>• Underwriting of issues.<br>• Corporate financial advisory, capital restructuring, and M&A consultancy.<br>• Portfolio management services (subject to separate SEBI PMS registration). | **₹50 Crore**<br>*(Enhanced from obsolete legacy ₹5 Cr)* | **₹12.5 Crore**<br>*(25% of Net Worth)* |

> **Implementation Timeline & Phased Compliance (SEBI Circulars Jan 2026 & 11 June 2026 Extension):**  
> • **New Applicants:** Must satisfy the full net worth and liquid net worth requirements immediately upon registration (Category I: ₹50 Crore / ₹12.5 Cr liquid; Category II: ₹10 Crore / ₹2.5 Cr liquid).  
> • **Existing Registrants (Glide Path):**  
>   - **Phase I (Interim Threshold):** Must achieve Net Worth of **₹25 Crore** and Liquid Net Worth of **₹6.25 Crore** by **31 March 2027** (as extended by SEBI Circular dated 11 June 2026).  
>   - **Phase II (Full Compliance):** Must achieve full compliance (**₹50 Crore** Net Worth / **₹12.5 Crore** Liquid Net Worth for Category I; **₹10 Crore** / **₹2.5 Crore** for Category II) by **2 January 2028**.  
>   - The legacy ₹5 Crore threshold is an **obsolete historical figure** and must not be treated as current law.

> **Crucial Regulatory Mandate:**  
> Only a **Category I Merchant Banker** is legally permitted to act as the **Lead Manager** to an Initial Public Offering (IPO) or rights issue on an Indian stock exchange!

### 3. Mandated Activities in Public Issue Management

• **Pre-Issue Obligations:**
  - Conducting comprehensive due diligence on the issuing company's financials, promoter background, and litigation.
  - Submitting the **Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP)** alongside a statutory **Due Diligence Certificate** to SEBI.
  - Appointing supporting issue intermediaries: Registrars to the Issue, Bankers to the Issue, Advertising Agencies, and Underwriters.
  - Organizing institutional investor roadshows and determining the price band via book-building.
• **Post-Issue Obligations:**
  - Monitoring subscription collections; ensuring compliance with the **minimum 90% subscription mandate** (if subscription falls below 90%, the issuer must refund entire application money within 4 days).
  - Finalizing basis of allotment in coordination with stock exchange authorities within **T+3 days**.
  - Submitting post-issue monitoring reports (initial report within 7 days, final report within 78 days) to SEBI.

---

### 4. SEBI Code of Conduct for Merchant Bankers

• Merchant bankers must observe high standards of integrity, dignity, and fairness in all dealings.  
• Must maintain **arms-length firewalls** to prevent conflict of interest between advisory clients.  
• Strictly prohibited from engaging in **insider trading or front-running** securities of corporate clients.  
• Must not make exaggerated statements, misleading claims, or guarantee assured returns to investors.

> **Core Proposition:** Factoring and forfaiting convert commercial trade receivables into immediate cash liquidity. The Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) institutionalizes MSME factoring on an electronic bidding platform without recourse to the MSME seller.

### 1. Factoring vs. Forfaiting

| Parameter | Factoring | Forfaiting |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Scope of Trade** | Typically used for **Domestic Trade Sales** (though international factoring exists). | Exclusively used for **Cross-Border International Export Trade**. |
| **Credit Term / Horizon** | **Short-term receivables** (typically 30 to 180 days). | **Medium to Long-term trade debts** (6 months up to 5–7 years). |
| **Recourse Nature** | Available as **With Recourse** OR **Without Recourse**. | **STRICTLY WITHOUT RECOURSE to the Exporter**. The forfaiter assumes 100% of the political and commercial default risk. |
| **Receivables Instrument** | Standard commercial sales invoices and book debts. | Negotiable trade instruments: Bills of Exchange and Promissory Notes guaranteed by the importer's bank (**Avalized**). |
| **Comprehensive Services** | Provides a bundle of services: sales ledger administration, debt collection, credit advisory, and financing. | Pure financial discounting transaction; zero ledger management. |

• **Factoring with Recourse:** If the debtor (buyer) fails to pay on maturity, the factor has legal recourse to recover the advanced funds from the client (seller).  
• **Factoring without Recourse:** The factor absorbs the credit default risk; if the debtor defaults, the factor cannot recover from the client.  
• **Factoring Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2021:** Liberalized factoring by permitting all NBFCs to register as factors, eliminating the requirement that factoring must constitute at least 50% of total assets and income.

---

### 2. Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS)

• **Regulatory Mandate & Platform Operator Eligibility:** Regulated under the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, based on RBI guidelines. Platform operating entities must maintain a minimum paid-up equity capital / net worth of **₹25 Crore**, robust IT infrastructure, and promoters experienced in financial markets or IT.  
• **Eligible Participants on TReDS:** Strictly tripartite: (1) **MSME Sellers** (Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises); (2) **Buyers** (Corporates, Central/State PSUs, Government departments/local bodies); (3) **Financiers** (Scheduled Commercial Banks, NBFC-Factors, and permitted financial institutions).  
• **Factoring Mechanics:** MSME uploads the digital invoice accepted by the buyer; financiers bid competitively via reverse auctions; MSME accepts the best bid for immediate liquidity.  
• **Crucial Rule:** Discounting on TReDS is executed **strictly WITHOUT RECOURSE to the MSME supplier**.

> **Core Proposition:** Equipment leasing and hire purchase finance industrial assets. In lease financing, legal ownership remains with the lessor throughout, whereas in hire purchase, ownership passes to the hirer upon clearance of the final installment.

### 1. Master Comparison: Lease Financing vs. Hire Purchase

| Parameter | Lease Financing | Hire Purchase |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Governing Statute** | **Indian Contract Act, 1872** & Transfer of Property Act, 1882 | **Indian Contract Act, 1872** & **Sale of Goods Act, 1930** (*Note: Hire-Purchase Act, 1972 was never brought into force and formally repealed by Repealing & Amending Act, 2005*). |
| **Ownership of Asset** | Remains with the **Lessor throughout** the contract period and upon expiry. | Passes to the **Hirer ONLY upon full payment of the last hire installment**. |
| **Depreciation Benefit** | Claimed by the **Lessor** on their balance sheet. | Claimed by the **Hirer** from the very first financial year. |
| **Tax Deductibility of Payments** | Lease rentals are tax-deductible as revenue expenditure in operating leases under income tax rules (subject to Ind AS 116). | Only the **finance charges (interest component)** are tax-deductible; the principal is a capital repayment. |
| **Initial Down Payment** | Typically **Zero down payment** (or small security deposit). | Mandates substantial upfront margin / down payment (**15% to 25%**). |
| **Termination Rights** | Financial leases are strictly non-cancellable. | Hirer can terminate before maturity by returning the goods. |

• **Leasing Regulatory Architecture & Asset Classes:** In Indian equipment leasing, dominant leased asset classes comprise **Plant & Machinery, Commercial Vehicles / Earthmoving Equipment, and IT / Office Automation Equipment**. Equipment leasing NBFCs are regulated by the RBI as **NBFC-ICCs** under the Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework. The legal relationship is governed by the bailment contract provisions of the **Indian Contract Act, 1872** and Transfer of Property Act, 1882.  
• **Ind AS 116 (Leases) & Financial Ratio Impacts:** Effective 1 April 2019, lessees must bring leases onto the balance sheet as a **Right-of-Use (ROU) Asset** and corresponding **Lease Liability** (exemptions apply to **short-term leases ≤ 12 months** and **leases of low-value assets**). Financial impacts: (1) **Higher EBITDA** (lease rental split into depreciation and finance cost); (2) **Higher Leverage** (debt-to-equity ratio increases due to recognized lease liabilities); (3) Front-loaded expense recognition.

> **Core Proposition:** Mutual funds pool retail savings into diversified portfolios under a four-tier trust structure (Sponsor, Trustee, AMC, Custodian). Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) pool private institutional capital into specialized venture, private equity, and hedge fund vehicles.

### 1. Mutual Funds Trust Architecture (SEBI Regulations, 1996)

1. **Sponsor:** The industrial/banking promoter establishing the fund (minimum 5-year track record in financial services; must contribute at least 40% of the AMC's net worth).
2. **Trust / Board of Trustees:** Holds the assets of the mutual fund in trust for the benefit of unit holders. At least **two-thirds of the Trustees must be independent**.
3. **Asset Management Company (AMC):** Manages the day-to-day investment portfolio of the mutual fund. Minimum Net Worth: **₹50 Crore**. At least **50% of the AMC Board must be independent directors**.
4. **Custodian:** Holds the physical and electronic custody of securities independent of the AMC and Sponsor.

• **Net Asset Value (NAV) Formula:**
  $$\text{NAV} = \frac{\text{Market Value of Investments} + \text{Current Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities and Provisions}}{\text{Total Number of Outstanding Units}}$$
  NAV is computed and published daily on business days by all mutual funds.

### 2. Mutual Fund Operational Tools: Scheme Categorization, Riskometer & Loads

• **Scheme Structures & Categorization (SEBI):** By structure: **Open-ended** (perpetual entry/exit at NAV), **Close-ended** (fixed maturity, listed on exchange), and **Interval schemes** (transaction windows). By asset class: 5 broad categories: **Equity, Debt, Hybrid, Solution-Oriented, and Other schemes (Index Funds/ETFs)**.  
• **New Fund Offer (NFO):** Initial public subscription period for a newly created mutual fund scheme; under revised SEBI directions, an NFO must remain open for a minimum of **3 working days** and a maximum of **15 calendar days** (ELSS schemes follow applicable Government scheme guidelines).  
• **SEBI Riskometer:** Dynamic risk grading tool updated monthly, displaying risk across **6 standardized tiers**: (1) Low, (2) Low to Moderate, (3) Moderate, (4) Moderately High, (5) High, and (6) Very High.  
• **Total Expense Ratio (TER) & Loads:**  
  - **Entry Load:** **Strictly PROHIBITED (0%)** by SEBI across all schemes since August 2009.  
  - **Exit Load:** Charged if units are redeemed before a specified period (e.g. 1 year); proceeds are credited back to the scheme.  
  - **TER Caps (Regulation 52):** Annual management and operational expenses are capped on a sliding scale based on AUM (equity schemes capped from 2.25% down to 1.05%; additional 30 bps allowed for inflows from Beyond-30 (B-30) cities).  
• **Investment Styles:** *Active Management* (beating benchmark through stock picking) vs. *Passive Management* (index funds and ETFs mimicking benchmark with minimal tracking error); *Growth* (earnings momentum) vs. *Value* (undervalued assets with safety margin).

---

### 3. Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) — Three SEBI Categories & Quantitative Baselines

Regulated under the **SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012**:

| Category | Permissible Fund Types & Objective | Leverage & Regulatory Stance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Category I AIF** | **Venture Capital Funds, SME Funds, Social Venture Funds, Infrastructure Funds.** Funds that invest in sectors viewed by government as economically beneficial. | Cannot borrow or employ leverage except for temporary working capital (max 30 days, max 10% of investible funds). Eligible for tax pass-through status. |
| **Category II AIF** | **Private Equity (PE) Funds, Debt Funds, Real Estate Funds, Funds of Funds.** Standard private investment vehicles. | Cannot employ leverage except for meeting temporary operational requirements (max 30 days). Eligible for tax pass-through status. |
| **Category III AIF** | **Hedge Funds, PIPE Funds, Complex Derivative Trading Funds.** Employs diverse and complex trading strategies. | **Permitted to employ leverage** and complex derivative strategies (subject to SEBI gross exposure cap of 2 times the NAV). |

• **AIF Core Quantitative Baselines:**
  - **Minimum Scheme Corpus:** At least **₹20 Crore** for each scheme of Category I, Category II, and Category III AIFs (except **Angel Funds**, where the minimum corpus is **₹5 Crore**).
  - **Minimum Investment Ticket Size:** Standard Investors: Minimum **₹1 Crore** per investor. Employees/Directors of AIF: Minimum **₹25 Lakh**. Angel Funds: Minimum **₹25 Lakh** per angel investor.
  - **Maximum Investor Headcount:** Capped at **1,000 investors** per scheme (except Angel Funds, capped at **200 angel investors**).
  - **Sponsor / Manager Continuing Interest ('Skin in the Game'):** Category I & II: At least **2.5% of corpus or ₹5 Crore**, whichever is lower. Category III: At least **5.0% of corpus or ₹10 Crore**, whichever is lower.
  - **Fund Tenure:** Categories I and II are strictly **close-ended** with a minimum tenure of **3 years**. Category III funds may be open-ended or close-ended.

---51:T1e81,> **Curriculum Alignment — Official IIBF Paper 1 Benchmark (Unit 45)**  
> **Core Proposition:** REITs and InvITs enable institutional and retail investors to invest in income-generating commercial real estate and infrastructure assets. At least 80% of assets must be in completed revenue-generating projects, with a mandatory 90% cash flow distribution requirement.

### 1. Core Operating Mandates for REITs & InvITs

• **Asset Composition Rule:** At least **80% of the aggregate value of assets** must be invested in **completed, revenue-generating commercial real estate or infrastructure projects**. A maximum of **20%** may be held in under-construction properties, equity of listed entities, or debt.  
• **Mandatory Distribution of Cash Flows:** Both REITs and InvITs must distribute at least **90% of their Net Distributable Cash Flows (NDCF)** to unit holders at least once every six months (quarterly for REITs).  
• **REIT vs. Real Estate Mutual Funds (REMF):** REITs directly acquire and lease physical commercial real estate (≥ 80% completed rent-generating assets; mandatory 90% NDCF payout; trade like equities). In contrast, REMFs (under SEBI Mutual Fund rules) do not manage physical properties; they invest in shares/debt of real estate companies or listed REIT units.  
• **InvIT Revenue Architecture:** Concession SPVs operate toll roads, transmission lines, or pipelines. Tolls, fixed annuities, or wheeling tariffs collected by SPVs are passed to the InvIT as interest and dividends; the InvIT distributes **≥ 90% of Net Distributable Cash Flows (NDCF)** to unitholders.  
• **Borrowing Leverage Norms & SEBI 2026 InvIT Nuance:**
  - *Standard Baseline:* Aggregate consolidated net debt of a REIT or InvIT cannot exceed **49% of the total value of assets** (if borrowings exceed 25%, credit rating and unitholder approval are mandatory).
  - *InvIT Borrowing Exception (SEBI Framework & May 15, 2026 Circular):* An InvIT is permitted to leverage beyond 49% up to a maximum ceiling of **70% of asset value**, provided it satisfies strict prudential conditions: (1) consolidated debt must hold a **mandatory 'AAA' (or equivalent) credit rating**; (2) track record of at least **6 consecutive distributions** to unitholders; (3) prior approval of unitholders with a **supermajority of at least 75% by value**; and (4) **strictly delimited permitted use**: fresh borrowing above 49% is restricted solely to (i) acquisition of infrastructure projects, (ii) capex/development of underlying projects, or (iii) refinancing of existing debt.

### 2. Taxation Framework for REITs and InvITs

• **Pass-Through Status (Section 115UA, Income-tax Act, 1961 / operative framework under Income-tax Act, 2025):** Income stream received by the Business Trust is passed through to unitholders retaining its original character:  
  - *Interest from SPVs:* Passed through tax-free to the Trust, taxable in unitholders' hands at applicable income tax slab rates.  
  - *Dividends from SPVs:* Tax-exempt in unitholders' hands if the SPV has not opted for concessional corporate tax under Section 115BAA; taxable if SPV opted for 115BAA.  
• **Capital Gains on Sale of Listed Units (Section 111A / 112A legacy framework; current tax regime):**  
  - **Short-Term Capital Gains (STCG):** Units held $\le$ 12 months taxed at **20%** (Section 111A).  
  - **Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG):** Units held > 12 months taxed at **12.5%** on gains exceeding ₹1.25 Lakh (Section 112A).

1. **Trap — Forfaiting Recourse:** Forfaiting is **STRICTLY WITHOUT RECOURSE** to the exporter. The forfaiter assumes 100% of the commercial default risk.

8. **Trap — SEBI Riskometer Tiers:** The SEBI Riskometer consists of **6 distinct risk tiers** (Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High, Very High), updated monthly.
9. **Trap — REIT/InvIT Unit Capital Gains Rates:** Under current tax law, STCG on listed units is taxed at **20%**, and LTCG (holding > 12 months) is taxed at **12.5%** on gains above ₹1.25 Lakh.

### Unit 37, 38, 39, 41 & 45 Practice Questions (IIBF DB&F Pattern)

### Answer Key & Explanations

• **Q1 — Answer: C.** Category III AIFs (such as hedge funds) are permitted by SEBI to employ leverage, whereas Categories I and II cannot.

> **Core Proposition:** Debt instruments are evaluated by SEBI-regulated Credit Rating Agencies (CRAs), while retail borrower credit histories are compiled by RBI-regulated Credit Information Companies (CICs) into 300–900 numerical scores.

### 1. Credit Rating Agencies (CRAs) — Regulated by SEBI

• **Governing Statute:** SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, **1999**.  
• **Leading CRAs in India:** CRISIL (established 1987, oldest CRA), ICRA (1991), CARE Ratings (1993), India Ratings and Research (Fitch group), Acuité Ratings, and Infomerics.  
• **Standard Long-Term Rating Scale:**
  - *Investment Grade:* `AAA` (Highest safety), `AA` (High safety), `A` (Adequate safety), and **`BBB` (Moderate safety)**.  
    **Crucial Exam Point:** **`BBB-` is the absolute lowest investment-grade rating**.
  - *Speculative / Non-Investment Grade (Junk):* Begins at **`BB+`**, followed by `BB`, `B`, `C` (High risk of default), and **`D` (Default status)**.
• **Rating Outlook & Fee Architecture:** CRAs issue a **Rating Outlook** (Positive, Stable, Negative, Watch). Under the standard **Issuer-Pays Model**, conflicts of interest are mitigated through independent rating committees, mandatory lead analyst rotation, and public fee disclosures.

### 2. Credit Information Companies (CICs) — Regulated by the RBI

• **Governing Statute:** Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, **2005 (CICRA 2005)**.  
• **The Four Licensed CICs:** (1) TransUnion CIBIL, (2) Experian India, (3) Equifax India, and (4) CRIF High Mark.  
• **The Credit Score:** A three-digit numerical score ranging strictly between **300 and 900**. A score of **750 and above** is generally considered good creditworthiness for commercial bank loan sanctions.  
• **Statutory Consumer Right:** Every citizen is legally entitled to **one free full credit report per calendar year** from each of the four licensed CICs.

---53:T123b,> **Curriculum Alignment — Official IIBF Paper 1 Benchmark (Unit 42)**  
> **Core Proposition:** Insurance operates under fundamental legal doctrines (*Uberrima Fides*, Insurable Interest, Indemnity). Commercial banks distribute policies under the 3+3+3 Bancassurance model, supported by IRDAI's Bima Trinity initiatives, social security covers (PMJJBY, PMSBY), and Insurance Ombudsman redressal.

### 1. Insurance Sector Architecture & Regulatory Milestones

• **Historical Evolution:** Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) formed by nationalizing 245 private insurers under the **LIC Act, 1956**. General insurance nationalized under the **General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972 (GIBNA)**, establishing the General Insurance Corporation of India (**GIC Re**, now the national reinsurer).  
• **Malhotra Committee (1994) & IRDA Act (1999):** Recommended opening the sector to private capital and establishing an independent regulator. **IRDAI** established as statutory apex regulator in April 2000. **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) Cap:** Under the *Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025* (in force **5 February 2026**), foreign investors are permitted to hold up to **100% equity capital** in Indian insurance companies (raised from the prior 74% ceiling).  
• **Key Metrics & Intermediaries:**  
  - **Insurance Penetration:** Ratio of total insurance premium to **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** in percentage.  
  - **Insurance Density:** Ratio of total premium to **total national population**, measured in USD per capita.  
  - **Insurance Repositories:** Licensed entities maintaining electronic insurance policies in e-Insurance Accounts (e-IA).

### 2. Fundamental Legal Principles of Insurance

| Principle | Legal Maxim | Operational Application & Legal Exception |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Utmost Good Faith** | *Uberrima Fides* | Both parties must fully disclose all material facts. Non-disclosure or misrepresentation renders the contract voidable. |
| **2. Insurable Interest** | Financial stake in the subject matter | The insured must suffer financial loss if the insured event occurs.<br>• *Life Insurance:* Must exist **at policy inception**.<br>• *Marine Insurance:* Must exist **at the time of loss**.<br>• *Fire Insurance:* Must exist **BOTH at inception AND at the time of loss**! |
| **3. Principle of Indemnity** | Restoration to exact financial status | Insured cannot make a profit from insurance; compensation is capped at the exact financial loss. **Strictly applies to General Insurance; DOES NOT apply to Life Insurance** (human life cannot be valued). |
| **4. Principle of Subrogation** | Step into shoes of the insured | Upon settling a total loss claim, the insurer acquires all legal rights to recover damages from third-party tortfeasors. |
| **5. Proximate Cause** | *Causa Proxima* | The active, efficient cause setting in motion the chain of events leading to loss; insurer is liable only if the proximate cause is an insured peril. |

### 3. Bancassurance, Micro-Insurance & The Bima Trinity

• **Open Architecture (IRDAI Regulations):** Commercial banks acting as Corporate Agents can tie up with up to **nine insurers**: $$\mathbf{3 \text{ Life}} + \mathbf{3 \text{ General}} + \mathbf{3 \text{ Standalone Health}}$$. Coercive cross-selling is strictly banned.  
• **Group vs. Micro-Insurance:** Group policies cover homogenous groups under a single master contract without individual medical underwriting. **Micro-Insurance** (under IRDAI micro-insurance regulations) provides low-income families with affordable coverage (sum assured ₹10,000–₹1,00,000, simplified policy issuance, and accelerated claim settlements).  
• **Bima Trinity Initiatives:** **Bima Sugam** (digital marketplace portal), **Bima Vistaar** (bundled composite micro-insurance cover), and **Bima Vahak** (women-led grassroots distribution force).

### 4. Social Insurance Schemes & Ombudsman Mechanism

• **Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY):** 1-year renewable life term cover of **₹2 Lakh** for death due to any reason; eligible for age **18 to 50 years**; annual premium of **₹436**.  
• **Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY):** 1-year renewable accidental death and disability cover of **₹2 Lakh** (₹1 Lakh for partial permanent disability); eligible for age **18 to 70 years**; annual premium of **₹20**.  
• **Insurance Ombudsman Framework:** Resolves individual policyholder grievances without legal costs. Pecuniary compensation award jurisdiction capped at **₹30 Lakh**. Award is **binding on the insurance company**.

---54:T1634,> **Curriculum Alignment — Official IIBF Paper 1 Benchmark (Unit 43)**  
> **Core Proposition:** Pension schemes provide post-retirement financial security under PFRDA regulation. The National Pension System (NPS) enforces model-specific exit guidelines, Atal Pension Yojana (APY) provides guaranteed minimum pensions, and the Unified Pension Scheme (UPS) introduces assured defined benefits for government employees.

### 1. National Pension System (NPS Architecture under PFRDA)

• **Tier-I Account:** Mandatory permanent retirement account; tax benefits under Sections 80CCD(1), 80CCD(1B) (additional ₹50,000 deduction), and 80CCD(2).  
• **Tier-II Account:** Voluntary withdrawable savings facility with zero lock-in (no special tax deductions).

### 2. PFRDA Sector & Model-Specific Exit & Withdrawal Framework (16 Dec 2025 Regulations & 2026 Guidelines)

Under PFRDA regulations and master guidelines, exit and withdrawal rules are strictly distinguished across three distinct subscriber models:

| Dimension / Event | Government Sector (Central/State Govt) | All-Citizen Model (Individual Voluntary) | Corporate Model (Employer-Employee) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Normal Exit Timing** | At Superannuation / Retirement / Discharge | At or after age 60 (deferrable up to age 85) | At age 60 or employer retirement age (up to age 85) |
| **Normal Annuitization vs Lump Sum** | • Min **40% Annuitized**<br>• Up to **60% Lump Sum** | • Min **20% Annuitized**<br>• Up to **80% Lump Sum** | • Min **20% Annuitized**<br>• Up to **80% Lump Sum** |
| **Normal Exit Small Corpus (100% Lump Sum)** | **Corpus ≤ ₹8 Lakh**<br>100% lump sum option *(for > ₹8L to ₹12L, special split applies; > ₹12L standard min 40% annuity)* | **Corpus ≤ ₹8 Lakh**<br>100% lump sum / SLW / SUR option *(Special band exists for ₹8L–₹12L)* | **Corpus ≤ ₹8 Lakh**<br>100% lump sum option *(PFRDA non-govt unified threshold)* |
| **Premature Exit Timing** | Resignation / Removal from service | Before age 60 (voluntary exit; 5-yr lock-in removed) | Before retirement / superannuation (voluntary exit) |
| **Premature Annuitization vs Lump Sum** | • Min **80% Annuitized**<br>• Up to **20% Lump Sum** | • Min **80% Annuitized**<br>• Up to **20% Lump Sum** | • Min **80% Annuitized**<br>• Up to **20% Lump Sum** |
| **Premature Small Corpus (100% Lump Sum)** | **Corpus ≤ ₹5 Lakh**<br>100% lump sum option *(PFRDA Schedule I)* | **Corpus ≤ ₹5 Lakh**<br>100% lump sum option *(PFRDA FAQs)* | **Corpus ≤ ₹5 Lakh**<br>100% lump sum option *(PFRDA non-govt unified threshold)* |
| **Post-60 Continuation & Deferral** | Annuity can be deferred up to age 85 | Can continue contributing and defer annuity/lump sum up to age 85 | Can continue contributing and defer annuity/lump sum up to age 85 |
| **Demise / Death of Subscriber** | 100% payout to nominee or legal heirs (or option for annuity) | 100% payout to nominee or legal heirs (or option for annuity) | 100% payout to nominee or legal heirs (or option for annuity) |

• **Partial Withdrawals (Tier-I Account):** Eligible after **3 years** continuous subscription; maximum **25% of subscriber's own contributions** (excluding employer contributions and returns). Under current PFRDA All-Citizen / Corporate guidelines, permitted up to **4 times** during entire tenure before age 60 with a minimum interval of 4 years between consecutive withdrawals (the 4-year interval is relaxed for designated medical emergencies / critical illnesses). Post-60, Systematic Unit Redemption (SUR) provides recurring liquidity.

### 3. Statutory Provident Funds & Annuity Framework

• **Employees' Provident Fund (EPF):** Governed by the **EPF & MP Act, 1952** for enterprises with 20+ workers. Employee contributes **12% of basic wage + DA**. Employer contributes **12%**, bifurcated into:  
  $$\mathbf{8.33\% \text{ into Employees' Pension Scheme (EPS)}} \quad\Big|\quad \mathbf{3.67\% \text{ into EPF}}$$  
  *Statutory Wage Ceiling Caveat:* The 8.33% EPS contribution is subject to a statutory wage ceiling of **₹15,000 per month** (maximum employer EPS contribution of **₹1,250 per month**); any employer contribution on salary exceeding ₹15,000 is diverted entirely into the employee's EPF account. (Additional 0.5% paid by employer towards EDLI life insurance).  
• **Public Provident Fund (PPF):** 15-year statutory maturity; enjoy complete **Exempt-Exempt-Exempt (EEE)** tax status; sovereign guarantee; minimum deposit **₹500**, maximum **₹1,50,000** per financial year.  
• **Annuity Types:** (1) *Immediate Annuity* (payout begins right after lump-sum purchase) vs *Deferred Annuity* (accumulates capital during deferment phase before payouts); (2) *Life Annuity with Return of Purchase Price (ROPP)* (pays regular annuity until demise, then returns initial principal purchase price to designated nominees).

---

### 4. Atal Pension Yojana (APY) & Unified Pension Scheme (UPS)

• **Atal Pension Yojana (APY):** Administered by PFRDA for citizens aged **18 to 40 years**; guarantees fixed monthly pension of **₹1,000, ₹2,000, ₹3,000, ₹4,000, or ₹5,000** starting at age 60; *income-tax payers are strictly ineligible* to enroll (effective 1 October 2022).  
• **Unified Pension Scheme (UPS):** Central Government scheme effective 1 April 2025: (1) **Assured Pension:** **50% of average basic pay** drawn in last 12 months (qualifying service ≥ 25 years; proportionate for 10–25 years); (2) **Assured Family Pension:** **60%** of employee pension; (3) **Assured Minimum Pension:** **₹10,000 per month** upon superannuation (min 10 years service).

> **Core Proposition:** Commercial banks undertake para-banking activities (credit cards, primary dealership, mutual fund distribution) under strict RBI net-worth thresholds and equity investment caps, with mandatory disclosure in their annual financial accounts.

### 1. Net Worth Thresholds & Prudential Investment Limits

• **Credit Card Business:** Scheduled Commercial Banks must maintain an independent **Net Worth of at least ₹100 Crore** to issue credit cards.  
• **Primary Dealership (PD) Business:** Departmental PD in G-Secs requires: (1) Min Net Owned Funds (NOF) of **₹1,000 Crore**, (2) Min CRAR of **9.0%** (bank-level Basel III capital adequacy norm; Standalone PDs require **15.0%** CRAR and ₹150 Cr NOF), (3) Net NPAs ≤ **3.0%**, and (4) Track record of net profit over preceding 3 consecutive financial years.  
• **Prudential Caps on Bank Investments in Subsidiaries:** Maximum **10% of paid-up capital and reserves** in a single financial subsidiary/JV; maximum **20%** across all subsidiaries, JVs, and financial entities combined.  
• **Mandatory Disclosure in Accounts:** Banks must disclose in the **"Notes to Accounts"** of their annual balance sheet all commissions, fees, and brokerages earned from distributing insurance, mutual funds, and third-party financial products.

### Examiner Trap Vault: Unit 40, 42, 43 & 44 High-Yield Distractors

1. **Trap — Lowest Investment Grade Rating:** **`BBB-`** is the lowest investment-grade rating. An option stating `BB+` is **incorrect** (`BB+` is speculative/junk grade).
2. **Trap — Insurable Interest in Fire Insurance:** Insurable interest in Fire Insurance must exist **BOTH at policy inception AND at the time of loss**. In Life Insurance, it is required only at policy inception.
3. **Trap — NPS Normal Exit Small Corpus & Deferral by Model:** Under PFRDA amended exit regulations, for **Both Government Sector and Non-Government sectors (All-Citizens & Corporate)**, if accumulated NPS corpus at retirement/age 60 is **≤ ₹8 Lakh**, the subscriber can withdraw **100% as a lump sum without mandatory annuitization** (for Government > ₹8L to ₹12L, special split applies; above ₹12L, min 40% annuity; for All-Citizens & Corporate above ₹12L, min 20% annuity). Both models allow continuation/deferral up to **age 85** (extended from age 75).
4. **Trap — NPS Premature Exit & Lock-in by Model:** In premature exit (resignation before superannuation / before age 60), min 80% annuity is mandatory. 100% full lump sum is permitted if corpus is **≤ ₹5 Lakh across both Government and Non-Government (All-Citizens & Corporate) sectors** (raised from legacy ₹2.5 Lakh). The previous 5-year lock-in for All-Citizens has been removed; partial withdrawals are permitted up to **4 times** before age 60.
5. **Trap — APY Income Tax Exclusion:** Income-tax payers are **STRICTLY INELIGIBLE** to enroll in Atal Pension Yojana.
6. **Trap — Credit Card Bank Net Worth:** Banks must have a minimum Net Worth of **₹100 Crore** to undertake standalone credit card issuance.
7. **Trap — Insurance Penetration vs Density:** Penetration is premium as a **% of GDP**; Density is premium **per capita in USD**. Do not reverse these two metrics.
8. **Trap — Social Insurance Premiums:** PMJJBY annual premium is **₹436** (life cover ₹2 Lakh); PMSBY annual premium is **₹20** (accidental cover ₹2 Lakh).
9. **Trap — Insurance Ombudsman Pecuniary Limit:** The Insurance Ombudsman can award compensation up to **₹30 Lakh** (including ex-gratia and other expenses).
10. **Trap — Employer EPF Contribution Split:** The employer's 12% is split into **8.33% to EPS** (capped at ₹15,000 wage ceiling, i.e., max ₹1,250/mo) and **3.67% + excess over ceiling into EPF**; it is NOT an unconditional 8.33% on uncapped salaries.
11. **Trap — Insurance FDI Ceiling:** Under the *Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025* (in force 5 February 2026), the statutory FDI ceiling in Indian insurance companies is **100%**, NOT 74% (and not 49%).

---57:T306e,1. **Trap 01 — Year of the Great Divide:** In Indian demography, **1921** is the Year of the Great Divide (mortality fell, population turned positive), NOT 1951.
2. **Trap 02 — Demographic Stage:** India is in **Stage 3 (Late Expanding)** with TFR at 2.0 (below 2.1 replacement level).
3. **Trap 03 — 2008 GFC Exposure:** Indian banks had **negligible direct exposure** to US subprime derivatives due to RBI prudential restrictions.
4. **Trap 04 — CGTMSE Ceiling & NITI Aayog Power:** CGTMSE collateral-free guarantee is **₹10 Crore per borrower** (NOT ₹5 Crore), managed by GoI and SIDBI. NITI Aayog has **ZERO fund allocation powers**; devolution rests with MoF.
5. **Trap 05 — 1st vs 2nd Plan:** 1st Plan used **Harrod-Domar** (agriculture); 2nd Plan used **Mahalanobis** (heavy capital goods).
6. **Trap 06 — Export Turnover in MSME:** Export turnover is **strictly excluded** when classifying Micro, Small, or Medium enterprises.
7. **Trap 07 — MSME Delayed Payment:** Penal interest is **3 times the Bank Rate compounded monthly**, NOT simple interest and NOT linked to Repo rate.
8. **Trap 08 — UCB PSL Target:** Under the 2025 revised framework, UCB overall target is **60% of ANBC**, NOT 75%.
9. **Trap 09 — HAM Traffic Risk:** In Hybrid Annuity Model road projects, the **Government absorbs 100% of the traffic risk**; private developer bears execution risk.
10. **Trap 10 — Net Zero Year:** India's Panchamrit commitment for Net Zero greenhouse emissions is **2070**, NOT 2050.
11. **Trap 11 — CSR Committee Exemption:** If CSR obligation is **≤ ₹50 Lakh**, no separate CSR committee is required; the Board discharges functions directly.
12. **Trap 12 — ICSID Membership:** India is **NOT a member** of the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID).
13. **Trap 13 — Current Account Convertibility:** Adopted under **Article VIII of IMF in August 1994**; full Capital Account convertibility is NOT implemented.
14. **Trap 14 — WTO Amber vs Green Box:** **Green Box subsidies are completely exempt** from reduction limits; Amber Box subsidies (MSP) are capped at 10% de minimis.
15. **Trap 15 — AIIB Shareholding:** India is the **second-largest shareholder** in AIIB after China.
16. **Trap 16 — GDP Base Year:** Current series is **Base Year 2022–23** (released 27 Feb 2026); 2011–12 is the historical previous series.
17. **Trap 17 — Official Definition of National Income:** Statistically defined as **Net National Product at Factor Cost ($\text{NNP}_{FC}$)**.
18. **Trap 18 — Transfer Payments:** Social pensions and scholarships are **EXCLUDED** from National Income because they generate no output.
19. **Trap 19 — ICOR Efficiency:** A **lower ICOR means higher capital productivity** (less capital needed per unit of GDP growth).
20. **Trap 20 — WPI Services Exclusion:** The Wholesale Price Index **DOES NOT include services**; services are tracked in CPI.
21. **Trap 21 — Inflation Anchor:** RBI MPC targets **Headline CPI-Combined ($4\% \pm 2\%$)**, NOT Core CPI and NOT WPI.
22. **Trap 22 — Minimum Reserve System Split:** ₹200 Cr total reserves = **min ₹115 Cr Gold** + ₹85 Cr Foreign Securities.
23. **Trap 23 — Post Office Exclusions:** National Savings Certificates (NSC) are **excluded** from $M4$ and $L1$.
24. **Trap 24 — Sweezy Oligopoly Kink:** Rivals **ignore price hikes** (elastic upper curve) but **match price cuts** (inelastic lower curve).
25. **Trap 25 — Rectangular Hyperbola Elasticity:** Price elasticity of demand is **equal to 1 (unitary) at every point** on a rectangular hyperbola curve.
26. **Trap 26 — Cross Elasticity Signs:** Substitutes have **positive** cross elasticity; Complements have **negative** cross elasticity.
27. **Trap 27 — Liquidity Trap Monetary Policy:** Inside a Liquidity Trap, **monetary policy is completely ineffective** (LM curve is horizontal); only fiscal policy works.
28. **Trap 28 — IS vs LM Curve Slopes:** IS curve slopes **downward**; LM curve slopes **upward**.
29. **Trap 29 — Word 'Budget' in Constitution:** The term "Budget" **does not appear** in the Constitution; it is the **'Annual Financial Statement' under Article 112**.
30. **Trap 30 — Plan vs Non-Plan Expenditure:** This classification was **formally abolished from FY 2017–18**; modern budgets use Capital vs Revenue.
31. **Trap 31 — Standing Deposit Facility (SDF):** RBI provides **zero collateral (uncollateralized)** to banks under SDF.
32. **Trap 32 — Contingency Fund Corpus:** Corpus is **₹30,000 Crore**, held by the Finance Secretary on behalf of the President.
33. **Trap 33 — Primary Deficit Zero Meaning:** If Primary Deficit = 0, then **Fiscal Deficit = Interest Payments**.
34. **Trap 34 — FSDC Leadership:** FSDC Apex Council is chaired by **Union Finance Minister**; FSDC Sub-Committee is chaired by **RBI Governor**.
35. **Trap 35 — IFSCA Scope:** IFSCA does not supersede domestic regulators across mainland India; remit is strictly inside **GIFT City IFSC**.
36. **Trap 36 — ₹1 Note Authority:** The ₹1 note and coins are issued by the **Ministry of Finance** (signed by Finance Secretary); notes ₹2 and higher are issued by **RBI under Section 22**.
37. **Trap 37 — Non-Banking Asset Disposal:** Maximum retention under BR Act Section 9 is **7 years + 5 years RBI extension = 12 years**.
38. **Trap 38 — Bank Reserve Fund Transfer:** Section 17 of BR Act states **20%**, but RBI Master Direction mandates **25% of net profit**.
39. **Trap 39 — Indian Minimum Basel III CRAR:** Total capital is **11.5% of RWAs** (9% CRAR + 2.5% CCB), exceeding BCBS 10.5%.
40. **Trap 40 — PCA Trigger Calibration:** PCA capital thresholds are measured as basis-point deterioration from the **regulatory baseline including CCB (11.5% CRAR / 8.0% CET1)**. Total CRAR Threshold 1 triggers at up to 250 bps below baseline (i.e., **9.0% to < 11.5%**); Threshold 2 is **7.5% to < 9.0%**; Threshold 3 is **< 7.5%**. For CET1, Threshold 1 is **6.375% to < 8.0%**; Threshold 2 is **4.875% to < 6.375%**; Threshold 3 is **< 4.875%**. Asset quality trigger is Net NPA $\ge 6.0\%$ (Threshold 1), $\ge 9.0\%$ (Threshold 2), $\ge 12.0\%$ (Threshold 3). RoA is officially removed.
41. **Trap 41 — D-SIBs in India:** The three Domestic Systemically Important Banks are **SBI, HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank**.
42. **Trap 42 — RRB Shareholding:** Central Government **50%**, Sponsor Bank **35%**, State Government **15%**.
43. **Trap 43 — Payment Bank Credit Prohibition:** Payment Banks **CANNOT lend, grant loans, or issue credit cards**. Maximum balance is **₹2,00,000**.
44. **Trap 44 — NBFC SBR Upper Layer:** The **Top 10 eligible NBFCs by asset size** are automatically placed in the Upper Layer.
45. **Trap 45 — Microfinance Household Income:** Uniform cap of **₹3,00,000 per annum** across both rural and urban areas. Collateral is strictly 0%.
46. **Trap 46 — First DFI in India:** **IFCI (1948)** was India's first DFI, NOT ICICI or IDBI.
47. **Trap 47 — CD vs CP Denomination:** Both Commercial Paper and Certificates of Deposit share the **same minimum denomination: ₹5 Lakh**.
48. **Trap 48 — Forfaiting vs Factoring Recourse:** Forfaiting is **strictly WITHOUT RECOURSE** to the exporter. TReDS factoring is also **strictly without recourse to MSME**.
49. **Trap 49 — Merchant Banker Net Worth (SEBI 2026 Dual Category):** Under SEBI Merchant Bankers (Amendment) Regulations effective 3 January 2026, Category I Merchant Bankers require minimum net worth of **₹50 Crore** (liquid net worth **₹12.5 Crore**). Category II requires net worth of **₹10 Crore** (liquid net worth **₹2.5 Crore**). Phased compliance under June 2026 extension (Phase I ₹25 Cr by 31 Mar 2027; Phase II full ₹50 Cr by 2 Jan 2028). Legacy ₹5 Crore is an obsolete historical figure.
50. **Trap 50 — NPS Exit Rules & Insurance FDI Ceiling:** (i) Under PFRDA amended exit regulations, for **Government Sector**, normal superannuation/retirement permits 100% lump sum up to **≤ ₹8 Lakh** (min 40% annuity above); premature/resignation allows 100% lump sum up to **≤ ₹5 Lakh** (min 80% annuity above). For **Non-Government sectors (Both All-Citizens and Corporate models)**, normal exit permits 100% lump sum up to **≤ ₹8 Lakh** (min 20% annuity above ₹12L; ₹8L–₹12L special split); premature exit allows 100% lump sum up to **≤ ₹5 Lakh** (min 80% annuity above). Continuation is permitted up to **age 85** (extended from 75); 5-year lock-in is removed; partial withdrawals allowed up to **4 times**. (ii) Under the *Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act, 2025* (in force 5 Feb 2026), the insurance FDI ceiling is **100%**, NOT 74%.

### § 27.3 Capstone Diagnostic Drill (Exam Simulation)

**Q1. [CONCEPT-RECURRING / 2026 BENCHMARK] An enterprise engaged in manufacturing has an investment in plant and machinery of ₹22 Crore, a domestic annual turnover of ₹85 Crore, and an export turnover of ₹60 Crore. Under the revised MSME classification criteria effective 1 April 2025, how is this enterprise classified?**  
A. Micro Enterprise  
B. Small Enterprise  
C. Medium Enterprise  
D. Large Corporate Enterprise  

**Q2. [PYQ-PATTERN / RECOLLECTED RECONSTRUCTION / 2026 BENCHMARK] Under the Reserve Bank of India's regulatory frameworks, which of the following pairs of financial instruments share the exact same statutory minimum denomination of ₹5 Lakh?**  
A. Treasury Bills and Commercial Paper  
B. Commercial Paper and Certificates of Deposit  
C. Certificates of Deposit and Inter-Corporate Deposits  
D. Cash Management Bills and Triparty Repos  

**Q3. [PYQ-PATTERN / RECOLLECTED RECONSTRUCTION] Under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, which of the following actions is STRICTLY PROHIBITED for a commercial banking company in India?**  
A. Operating safety deposit locker facilities for retail depositors  
B. Granting personal or commercial loans against the security of its own shares  
C. Acting as an agent for the distribution of mutual fund units on a non-risk basis  
D. Borrowing overnight funds in the interbank call money market  

**Q4. [CONCEPT-RECURRING / 2026 BENCHMARK] An All-Citizen / Non-Government subscriber to the National Pension System (NPS) attains the age of 60 years with an accumulated pension corpus of ₹7,40,000. Under current PFRDA exit regulations (as amended on 16 December 2025), the subscriber is legally entitled to:**  
A. Compulsorily convert at least 80% of the corpus into an immediate annuity  
B. Compulsorily convert at least 40% into an annuity and take 60% as a lump sum  
C. Withdraw 100% of the entire accumulated corpus as a lump sum without purchasing an annuity  
D. Forfeit the corpus to the Central Recordkeeping Agency due to failure to reach ₹10 Lakh  

**Q5. [PYQ-PATTERN / RECOLLECTED RECONSTRUCTION] In fixed-income portfolio management, what is the Macaulay Duration of a 10-year sovereign Zero-Coupon Bond?**  
A. 5.0 years  
B. 7.5 years  
C. Exactly 10.0 years  
D. Zero years  

---

### Answer Key & Explanations

• **Q1 — Answer: B.** Under the 1 April 2025 criteria, Small Enterprise thresholds are Investment $\le$ ₹25 Cr and Turnover $\le$ ₹100 Cr. Export turnover (₹60 Cr) is strictly excluded, leaving relevant turnover at ₹85 Cr (which is $\le$ ₹100 Cr). With investment at ₹22 Cr ($\le$ ₹25 Cr), the enterprise is classified as a **Small Enterprise**.  
• **Q2 — Answer: B.** Both Commercial Paper (CP) and Certificates of Deposit (CD) share the exact statutory minimum denomination of ₹5 Lakh under RBI directions.  
• **Q3 — Answer: B.** Section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 strictly prohibits any bank from making loans or advances on the security of its own shares.  
• **Q4 — Answer: C.** Under the PFRDA amended exit regulations (16 Dec 2025), for Non-Government / All-Citizens subscribers at normal exit (age 60), if the accumulated corpus is $\le$ ₹8 Lakh, the subscriber has the option to withdraw 100% of the corpus as a lump sum without mandatory annuitization. Because ₹7,40,000 is below the ₹8 Lakh threshold, Option C is correct.  
• **Q5 — Answer: C.** Because a zero-coupon bond pays zero intermediate coupons and returns all cash flow at final maturity, its Macaulay Duration mathematically equals its maturity period (10.0 years).

> **Core Proposition:** A company is an artificial legal person created by law, with perpetual succession and an optional common seal (under the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015, common seal is optional; documents can be signed by two directors or one director and the Company Secretary). Ultra vires transactions (beyond the Memorandum of Association) are void and cannot be ratified. Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates statutory registration of all charges created by a company within strict timeframes.

### 1. Types of Companies & Key Documents

| Entity Type | Minimum Members / Directors | Key Statutory Documents & Operational Rules |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Private Limited Company** | Min 2 Members / Max 200;<br>Min 2 Directors | • **Certificate of Incorporation** issued by ROC.<br>• **Memorandum of Association (MoA):** Defines the external boundary of company's powers and main objects (borrowing power clause).<br>• **Articles of Association (AoA):** Internal governance regulations, board meetings, delegation to directors. |
| **Public Limited Company** | Min 7 Members / No Max;<br>Min 3 Directors | • Requires Certificate of Incorporation.<br>• Share capital freely transferable.<br>• Can invite public deposits (subject to eligibility criteria under Section 76: net worth $\ge$ ₹100 Cr or turnover $\ge$ ₹500 Cr with credit rating) and issue listed debentures. |
| **One Person Company (OPC)** | Exactly 1 Member (Natural Person, Indian Citizen); Min 1 Director | • Sole member must nominate another natural person as **Nominee** in the event of death/incapacity.<br>• Simplified compliance; cannot carry on non-banking financial investment activities. |
| **Section 8 Company (Not-for-Profit)** | Min 2 Members (Private) / 7 (Public); Min 2/3 Directors | • Formed for promotion of commerce, art, charity, education.<br>• Prohibited from paying dividends to members.<br>• Profits must be applied solely to promoting its objects. |

### 2. Board Resolution & Authorized Signatories

Every corporate bank account opening or credit facility must be supported by a **Board Resolution** passed by the Board of Directors:
• Must be certified as a true copy by the Chairman / Company Secretary.
• Explicitly names authorized individuals, operating mandates (singly/jointly), borrowing limits, and authority to mortgage/pledge company property.
• **Doctrine of Indoor Management (*Royal British Bank v. Turquand*):** Outside parties dealing in good faith are entitled to presume that internal regulations have been complied with. However, the doctrine **does not protect a bank if there is actual knowledge of irregularity, forgery, or gross negligence**.

---5a:T8ed,> **P0 Audit Fix — Stop-Ship Regulatory Clearance (C-03)**  
> Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 imposes a statutory duty on every company creating a charge on its property or assets (tangible or intangible, in India or abroad) to register the particulars of the charge with the Registrar of Companies (ROC).

### 1. The Statutory Charge Registration Timeline (Section 77 & 87)

• **Normal Statutory Period (Section 77(1)):**
  - Registration within **30 days** of the date of creation of charge.
  - Normal prescribed filing fees payable via MCA portal (Form CHG-1 for assets other than debentures, Form CHG-9 for debentures).
• **First Extension by Registrar (First Proviso to Section 77(1)):**
  - If not registered within 30 days, the Registrar may, on application, allow registration to be made within a period of **sixty (60) days of such creation**.
  - Permitted upon payment of prescribed **additional fees**.
• **Second Extension by Registrar on Ad Valorem Fees (Second Proviso to Section 77(1)):**
  - If not registered within the 60-day period from creation, the Registrar may allow registration within a **further period of sixty (60) days**.
  - Permitted upon application and payment of prescribed **ad valorem fees** based on the value of the charge.
  - **Total Outer Window with RoC:** Exactly **120 days from creation** (60 days from creation + further 60 days).
• **Condonation of Delay by Central Government (Section 87):**
  - Beyond 120 days from the date of creation of the charge, the **Registrar has zero statutory power** to register the charge.
  - The company or any interested person (such as the lending bank) must petition the Central Government (delegated to the Regional Director) under Section 87 for condonation of delay and rectification of the register.

### 2. Consequences of Non-Registration (Section 77(3))

If a charge is not registered with the ROC:
• The charge is **VOID against the Liquidator and any other Creditor** of the company.
• If the company enters insolvency or liquidation, the bank is treated as an **unsecured creditor**, losing its priority over the secured asset!
• **Protection of the Debt:** Non-registration does NOT invalidate the underlying debt. The money secured remains payable immediately.

> **Core Proposition:** Inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits are subject to statutory transfer to the Depositor Education and Awareness (DEA) Fund under Section 26A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Attachment orders served by Civil Courts and Tax Authorities impose strict legal duties on bankers.

### 1. Inoperative Accounts & Unclaimed Deposits (DEA Fund Architecture)

• **Inoperative / Dormant Account Definition:**
  - An account is classified as **inoperative (dormant)** if there are **no customer-induced transactions for a continuous period of 2 years**.
  - Customer-induced transactions include cash deposit/withdrawal, cheque clearance, ATM/POS debit, Internet/Mobile banking transfer, and standing instructions.
  - Bank-induced transactions (interest credit, annual service charges debit) **DO NOT prevent an account from becoming inoperative**.
• **RBI Operational Safeguards on Inoperative Accounts:**
  - Banks **CANNOT levy any penal charges** for non-maintenance of minimum balance on inoperative accounts.
  - Savings account interest **must continue to be credited** regularly, regardless of inoperative status.
  - Reactivation of an inoperative account must be done **completely free of cost** upon fresh customer KYC verification.
• **Unclaimed Deposits & The DEA Fund (Section 26A, BR Act, 1949):**
  - Any deposit account remaining inoperative or unclaimed for **10 years or more** (or term deposits unclaimed for 10 years after maturity date) must be transferred to the **Depositor Education and Awareness (DEA) Fund** maintained by the Reserve Bank of India.
  - Balances must be transferred along with accrued interest by the end of the following month.
  - **UDGAM Portal (Unclaimed Deposits - Gateway to Access inforMation):** Centralized web portal launched by RBI allowing public to search for unclaimed deposits across multiple banks in one centralized window.
  - Depositors retain the statutory right to claim refund of their funds with interest from their bank at any time, which the bank settles and reclaims from the DEA Fund.

---5e:T7e8,### 1. Master Comparative Framework

| Dimension | Garnishee Order (CPC Order XXI Rule 46) | Income Tax Attachment (IT Act Sec 226(3) / 2025 Transition)* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Issuing Authority** | Competent Civil Court execution of money decree. | Tax Recovery Officer (TRO) / Assessing Officer. |
| **Procedural Stages** | Two-stage: Order Nisi (interim) & Order Absolute. | Single administrative attachment notice. |
| **Scope of Attachment** | Strictly debts **"due or accruing due"** at moment of service. Does NOT attach future credits. | Attaches money due **AND "money that may become due"** subsequently until tax debt is satisfied. |
| **Joint Account Operation** | Order against A alone **CANNOT attach joint account (A & B)**. | Attaches proportionate share of debtor unless proven otherwise. |
| **Sovereign Priority** | Subordinate to government tax attachments. | Priority as Crown Debt; takes precedence over civil Garnishee, **BUT cannot override prior pledge/lien**. |

*\*Statutory Transition Note:* Section 226(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 represents the classic statutory garnishee authority tested in banking examinations. Following the repeal of the 1961 Act effective 1 April 2026, identical continuing attachment powers are preserved and mapped into the recovery provisions of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

### 2. Legal Scope: Debts "Due or Accruing Due"

• A Garnishee Order attaches only debts belonging to the judgment debtor that are either **due immediately** (payable on demand, e.g., current/savings balances) or **accruing due** (an existing obligation payable on a future date, e.g., Fixed Deposit maturing in 6 months).
• **Items NOT Attached by Garnishee Order:**
  - Cheques deposited by customer but not yet cleared/credited.
  - Money held by bank in trust or as a bailee.
  - Overdraft limits or unutilized credit limits (an undrawn loan limit is not a debt owed by bank to customer).
  - Subsequent credits received after the exact moment of service of the Order Nisi.

> Previously, Section 45ZA of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 permitted only a **single nominee** for an individual deposit account. On **1 November 2025**, the **Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025** came into force, radically modernizing nomination rights.

### 1. Reconciled Nomination Rules: 2025 Statutory Baseline

| Deposit / Facility Type | Previous Statutory Rule (Pre-2025) | REVISED STATUTORY LAW (Banking Laws Amendment Act, 2025) | Operational Guidelines |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Deposit Accounts** (Savings, Current, FD, RD) | Only **ONE** nominee permitted per individual account. | • **Simultaneous Nomination:** Up to **FOUR (4) NOMINEES** permitted simultaneously.<br>• **Successive Nomination:** Account holder may specify nominees in succession.<br>• Customer defines percentage share for each simultaneous nominee (totaling 100%). | Nominee gets valid discharge of bank's liability; acts as trustee for legal heirs. |
| **Safe Deposit Lockers (Sole Hirer)** | Only **ONE** nominee permitted. | Up to **FOUR (4) nominees** permitted simultaneously or successively. | Nominee receives access to locker contents and can inventory/remove items. |
| **Safe Deposit Lockers (Joint Hirers)** | Maximum **TWO** nominees permitted. | Modernized survivor/nominee access framework allows seamless handover. | Access granted jointly to survivor(s) and nominee(s) of deceased hirer. |
| **Safe Custody Articles** | Only **ONE** nominee permitted. | Successive and simultaneous nomination framework extended. | Bank obtains full legal discharge upon delivery to validated nominee. |

### 2. Legal Status of Nominee vs. Legal Heir

• A nominee is **NOT an absolute owner** of the deposit funds or locker contents.
• Settled Supreme Court Law (*Sarojini Amma v. Neelakanta Pillai* & *Ram Chander Talwar v. Devinder Kumar Talwar*):
  - Nomination confers only the **right to receive payment** from the bank.
  - The nominee holds the funds as an **Agent / Trustee for the legal heirs** of the deceased under the applicable law of succession (Hindu Succession Act, Indian Succession Act, etc.).
  - Payment to the nominee gives the bank **complete and valid statutory discharge** against claims by legal heirs under Section 45ZA(2) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

---61:T558,### 1. Banker's Liability & Compensation Framework

• **Lessor-Lessee Relationship:** Hiring a safe deposit locker creates a **Lessor (Bank) and Lessee (Customer)** relationship, NOT bailor-bailee. The customer has exclusive physical access to the contents via his key; the bank holds the master key and has no knowledge of what is stored.
• **100x Liability Cap (RBI Revised Locker Directions):**
  - For incidents such as fire, theft, burglary, robbery, building collapse, or **fraud committed by bank employees**:
  - The bank's liability is strictly capped at **100 times the prevailing annual rent** of the locker.
  - The bank is **NOT liable** for damage/loss caused by natural calamities (floods, earthquakes, lightning) or customer negligence.
• **Term Deposit Security for Lockers:**
  - To ensure prompt payment of locker rent, banks are permitted to obtain a Fixed Deposit covering up to **3 years of locker rent** plus estimated charges for breaking open the locker in case of default.
  - Banks **CANNOT demand excessive term deposits** or insist on fixed deposits from existing customers with satisfactory operations.
• **Settlement of Deceased Claims:**
  - Banks must settle claims and grant access to locker/deposit balances to nominees/survivors within **15 days** of receipt of claim form, death certificate, and identity verification.

### 1. The Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS)

• **Eligibility:** Resident Individuals (including minors, with guardian approval). Not available to Corporates, Partnership Firms, HUFs, or Trusts.

  - Going abroad for employment, emigration, maintenance of close relatives.

  - Opening foreign currency accounts abroad, purchasing property or shares abroad.
• **Prohibited Remittances:** Trading in foreign exchange abroad, purchase of lottery tickets, remittance for sweepstakes or banned magazines, margins for overseas derivatives trading.

> **Core Proposition:** Section 22 of the RBI Act gives the Reserve Bank the sole right to issue banknotes. The Clean Note Policy mandates circulation of good quality notes, banning stapling and writing on banknotes. Counterfeit note detection requires mandatory impounding and reporting.

### 1. Currency Chests & Clean Note Policy

• **Currency Chests:** Operating branches authorized by RBI to hold sovereign cash reserves. Funds in currency chests belong to the Reserve Bank of India, not the holding commercial bank.
• **Clean Note Policy Rules:**
  - Banning of stapling, pinning, or stitching of banknote packets.
  - Banks must issue only clean notes to the public and withdraw soiled/mutilated notes from circulation.
  - Bank staff and public are prohibited from scribbling or writing on the watermark area or security threads of banknotes.

### 2. Soiled, Mutilated & Imperfect Notes (RBI Note Refund Rules)

| Note Classification | Physical Condition Definition | Operational Exchange / Refund Entitlement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Soiled Note** | Notes that have become dirty due to normal circulation or cut into two pieces with both pieces belonging to the same note (forming a complete note). | **Exchanged at full value** at any bank branch across the counter without question. |
| **Mutilated Note** | Notes with a portion missing or composed of more than two pieces pasted together. | • **Denominations ₹50 and Above (₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500):**<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;- **Full Value:** Undivided single largest piece area is **> 80%**.<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;- **Half Value:** Area is **$\ge$ 40% and $\le$ 80%**.<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;- **Rejected (Zero Value):** Area is **< 40%**.<br>• **Denominations Up to ₹20 (₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20):**<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;- **Full Value:** Undivided single largest piece area is **> 50%**.<br>&nbsp;&nbsp;- **Rejected (Zero Value):** Area is **$\le$ 50%** (No half-value refund exists for denominations up to ₹20). |
| **Extremely Mutilated / Charred / Inseparable** | Notes burnt, charred, or stuck together that cannot be separated. | Cannot be exchanged across branch counters; must be forwarded to the designated Issue Department of the RBI for special adjudication. |

### 3. Detection & Impounding of Counterfeit Banknotes

• **Mandatory Impounding:** No bank branch or teller can return a suspected counterfeit note to the presenter or destroy it. The note must be stamped with **"COUNTERFEIT BANKNOTE IMPOUNDED"** in prescribed dimensions.
• **Receipt:** A designated receipt must be issued to the presenter, signed by both the customer and the bank cashier.
• **Police Reporting Framework:**
  - **Up to 4 Counterfeit Notes in a Single Transaction:** Consolidated monthly report sent to the local Nodal Police Station at the end of the month.
  - **5 or More Counterfeit Notes in a Single Transaction:** The bank must immediately lodge a First Information Report (**FIR**) with the local police for criminal investigation.

> **Core Proposition:** A negotiable instrument is a transferable document entitling the holder to an unconditional sum of money. Section 13 defines it as a promissory note, bill of exchange, or cheque payable either to order or to bearer.

### 1. The Triad of Negotiable Instruments

| Statutory Feature | Promissory Note (Section 4) | Bill of Exchange (Section 5) | Cheque (Section 6) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Number of Parties** | 2 (Maker and Payee) | 3 (Drawer, Drawee, Payee) | 3 (Drawer, Drawee Bank, Payee) |
| **Nature of Undertaking** | **Unconditional Promise** to pay. | **Unconditional Order** to pay. | **Unconditional Order** on a bank. |
| **Drawee Entity** | Maker himself is debtor. | Any person or corporate body. | Must **ALWAYS be a specified Bank**. |
| **Payable on Demand / Usance** | Can be on demand or usance. | Can be on demand or usance. | **ALWAYS payable on demand only**. |
| **Acceptance Required** | No acceptance required. | Must be accepted by Drawee. | No acceptance required. |
| **Grace Days** | 3 days grace for usance notes. | 3 days grace for usance bills. | **ZERO grace days**. |
| **Stamping** | Required under Stamp Act. | Required under Stamp Act. | **Statutorily EXEMPT from stamp duty**. |

### 2. Holder (Section 8) vs. Holder in Due Course (Section 9)

• **Holder (Sec 8):** Any person entitled in his own name to the possession of the instrument and to receive or recover the amount due thereon.
• **Holder in Due Course (HIDC - Sec 9):** A person who for **valuable consideration** became the possessor/payee/endorsee of an instrument:
  1. **Before maturity**.
  2. In **good faith** and without sufficient cause to believe that any defect existed in the title of the person from whom he derived it.
• **Privileges & Statutory Limits of HIDC (Sections 36, 42, 43, 58):**
  - **Better Title than Transferor:** An HDC acquires a title free from equities and prior defects. Under **Section 58**, even if an instrument was lost or obtained by fraud, offense, or unlawful consideration, an HDC can validly recover on it.
  - **Crucial Statutory Exception — Forgery Cannot be Cleansed:** HDC protection **does NOT cure a forged instrument**. A forged drawer signature or forged endorsement is a complete nullity (*null and void ab initio*); forgery confers zero title even to an HDC! Nor can an HDC enforce an instrument void ab initio under express statutory prohibitions (e.g., executed by an incompetent minor).
  - **Estoppel & Prior Liability:** Estoppel against denying original validity or payee's capacity; all prior parties remain liable to the HDC until the instrument is duly satisfied.

### 3. Crossing & Material Alteration (Sections 123–131, 87)

• **General Crossing (Sec 123):** Two parallel transverse lines across the face, with or without "and Company". Mandates payment **only through a bank**.
• **Special Crossing (Sec 124):** Name of a banker added across the face. Payable **only through the designated bank**.
• **Not Negotiable Crossing (Sec 130):** The person taking it **shall not have and cannot give a better title than that which the person from whom he took it had**. Transferability remains, but negotiability (title cleansing) is destroyed!
• **Material Alteration (Sec 87):** Any alteration that changes the legal character, date, sum payable, time, place of payment, or rate of interest. **Renders the instrument void** unless made with the consent of all parties.

### 4. Criminal Liability for Dishonour: Section 138 Framework

• **Operative Conditions:**
  1. Cheque presented within validity period (3 months from date of issue).
  2. Dishonoured due to **insufficiency of funds** or exceeds arrangement.
  3. Payee makes a demand for payment by giving a **written notice within 30 days** of receiving information/memo of dishonour from the bank.
  4. Drawer fails to make payment within **15 days** of receipt of notice.
  5. Complaint must be filed within **1 month** before the Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate First Class.
• **Statutory Penalties:** Imprisonment for a term which may extend to **two (2) years**, or with fine which may extend to **twice the amount of the cheque**, or with both.

---6c:Tbdc,> **Curriculum Alignment — Official IIBF Paper 2 Benchmark (Units 13 & 14)**  
> **Core Proposition:** A paying banker has a statutory duty under Section 31 to honour cheques if drawn properly against sufficient funds. Protection is available under Sections 10, 85, 85A, and 89. Collecting bankers enjoy statutory protection under Section 131 if collecting crossed cheques in good faith and without negligence.

### 1. Protection to the Paying Banker

| Statutory Section | Instrument Type Covered | Conditions Required for Statutory Protection |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Section 85(1)** | Order Cheques | Payment made in **due course** (Section 10); endorsement purports to be made by or under authority of payee. Bank not required to verify authenticity of payee endorsement. |
| **Section 85(2)** | Bearer Cheques | Payable to bearer; protected if paid in due course to the bearer, **notwithstanding any endorsement on the back**. *"Once a bearer cheque, always a bearer cheque."* |
| **Section 85A** | Bank Drafts | Draft drawn by one branch on another; protected if endorsement purports to be by or under authority of payee. |
| **Section 89** | Materially Altered Cheques | Protected if payment is made in good faith and without negligence, **provided the alteration is NOT apparent** on visual inspection. |
| **Section 128** | Crossed Cheques | Paying banker paying a crossed cheque in due course (to a bank for general crossing, or designated bank for special crossing) is deemed to have paid the true owner. |

> **Critical Legal Trap — Forgery of Drawer's Signature:**  
> The protection under Section 85 applies **ONLY to forged endorsements**. If the **drawer's signature is forged**, the mandate is void *ab initio*. A bank paying a cheque with a forged drawer signature has zero statutory protection and cannot debit the customer's account, regardless of how skillful the forgery was (*Bihta Cooperative Bank v. Bank of Bihar*).

### 2. Protection to the Collecting Banker (Section 131)

A collecting banker is an agent for collection and is liable under common law for conversion if collecting a stolen instrument. Section 131 grants statutory immunity provided four non-negotiable conditions are satisfied:
1. The cheque must be **crossed generally or specially** before it comes into the hands of the bank (bank cannot cross an uncrossed cheque to claim Section 131 protection).
2. The bank must collect the cheque as an **agent for a customer** (not as a holder for value).
3. The collection must be executed in **good faith**.
4. The collection must be executed **WITHOUT NEGLIGENCE**.
• **What Constitutes Negligence by Collecting Banker:**
  - Opening an account without proper KYC or address verification.
  - Collecting an 'Account Payee' crossed cheque for an account other than the named payee.
  - Crediting cheques drawn in favor of a company or partnership into the personal account of a director or partner without inquiry.
  - Failing to notice clear discrepancies in endorsements or amounts.

---6d:T5ff,### 1. Demand Drafts & Banker's Cheques

• **Demand Draft (DD):** An order drawn by one office of a bank upon another office of the same bank for payment of a specified sum to order.
  - Governed by Section 85A NI Act.
  - Validity is **3 months** from date of issue.
  - **Section 31, RBI Act Restriction:** Demand Drafts **CANNOT be issued payable to bearer on demand**. (Only RBI and Central Government can issue bearer demand instruments).
  - Drafts for **₹50,000 and above** cannot be issued against cash; must be funded through account debit.
• **Banker's Cheque (Pay Order):** Drawn on the issuing branch itself; payable locally within the clearing zone.

### 2. Electronic Remittance Systems: NEFT vs. RTGS

| Operational Feature | NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) | RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Settlement Architecture** | Deferred Net Settlement (DNS) in half-hourly batches (48 batches daily). | Real Time continuous gross settlement of each transaction individually. |
| **Operating Hours** | **24 x 7 x 365 days** (Round the clock). | **24 x 7 x 365 days** (Round the clock). |
| **Minimum Amount** | **No Minimum limit** (even ₹1 can be sent). | **MINIMUM ₹2,00,000 (₹2 Lakh)**. |
| **Maximum Amount** | No upper ceiling. | No upper ceiling. |
| **Indo-Nepal Scheme** | Supported up to ₹2 Lakh per transaction. | Not applicable. |
| **Beneficiary Credit TAT** | Next batch settlement (normally within 2 hours). | Real-time, within 30 minutes of settlement. |

---6f:T821,> **Curriculum Alignment — Official IIBF Paper 2 Benchmark (Unit 16)**  
> **Core Proposition:** Financial Inclusion is the process of ensuring access to financial services and timely, adequate credit where needed by vulnerable groups at an affordable cost (Rangarajan Committee, 2008). Anchored in the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), the framework utilizes Business Correspondents (BCs) and digital tools.

### 1. Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) & BSBDA Norms

• **Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account (BSBDA):**
  - **Zero Minimum Balance:** No requirement of maintaining any minimum balance.
  - **No Annual Maintenance Charges:** Basic RuPay Debit Card issued completely free of cost.
  - **Free Services:** Minimum 4 cash withdrawals per month free of charge (including ATM withdrawals). Unlimited free cash deposits.
  - **BSBDA-Small Accounts:** Relaxed KYC for individuals lacking standard OVDs: aggregate credits $\le$ ₹1 Lakh/year, aggregate withdrawals $\le$ ₹10,000/month, balance at any point $\le$ ₹50,000. Valid for 12 months, extendable by 12 months if applied for an OVD.
• **Special PMJDY Features:**
  - **Overdraft (OD) Facility:** Up to **₹10,000** available to one adult per eligible household (preferably the woman of the house) after 6 months of satisfactory account operation; OD up to **₹2,000 without any conditions**. Age limit: **18 to 65 years**.
  - **Accidental Insurance Cover:** Free accidental insurance cover of **₹2 Lakh** on RuPay cards issued to PMJDY accounts (provided the card was used at least once in 90 days).

### 2. Business Correspondents (BC) & RSETI Architecture

• **Business Correspondent (BC) Model:** Retail agents engaged by banks to provide doorstep banking services in unbanked rural/semi-urban areas using micro-ATMs and biometric Aadhaar authentication.
• **Rural Self Employment Training Institutes (RSETI):** Dedicated training centers managed by lead banks with Ministry of Rural Development support to provide free skill development and entrepreneurship training to rural youth.

---70:T93a,### 1. Key Customer Service Committees

• **Goiporia Committee (1990):** Recommended 15-minute counter service benchmarks, display of service charges, specialized teller systems, and mandatory training of frontline branch staff.
• **Damodaran Committee (2011):** Recommended zero penal charges on inoperative accounts, standardized basic services, third-party ATM fee limitations, and establishment of Chief Customer Service Officers (Internal Ombudsman) in banks.

### 2. Historical Status of BCSBI (Banking Codes and Standards Board of India)

> **Auditor Finding Fix — Historical Status Qualifier (H-06)**  
> • The **Banking Codes and Standards Board of India (BCSBI)** was set up in 2006 as an independent watchdog following the Tarapore Committee recommendations. It formulated two non-statutory voluntary codes:
>   1. *Code of Bank's Commitment to Customers*
>   2. *Code of Bank's Commitment to Micro and Small Enterprises*
> • **Current Legal Reality:** **BCSBI was formally dissolved and wound up in 2019**. The voluntary codes have been retired. Customer protection in Indian banking is now directly enforced through **statutory RBI Master Directions on Customer Service**, the **Internal Ombudsman scheme**, and the **Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 (RB-IOS)**.

### 3. Banker's Duty of Confidentiality & Legal Exceptions

Section 13 of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970/1980 and Section 44 of the SBI Act, 1955 mandate strict customer confidentiality (*Tournier* doctrine). Disclosures are permitted only under:
• **Compulsion of Law:** Income Tax Act 1961 (Sections 131, 133(6), 226(3)); Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 Section 94 (*earlier CrPC §91*); Section 12 PMLA 2002 (reporting CTR/STR to FIU-IND); orders under Bankers' Books Evidence Act 1891 / BSA 2023.
• **Credit Information Sharing:** Mandatory **fortnightly submission** of credit records to Credit Information Companies (CICs: CIBIL, Equifax, Experian, CRIF High Mark) under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. Under RBI directions (effective 1 January 2025), credit institutions must update credit information as of the 15th and last day of each month, submitting data within **seven (7) calendar days** of the reporting fortnight (replacing the historical monthly cadence).
